attempts.answer:
Summary answer
Yes. A growing body of LLM and LLM‑agent research explicitly operationalizes “privilege” through least‑privilege policies, capability isolation, access control, and gated tool use to make agents safer. Representative approaches include principled privilege‑separation frameworks (e.g., Prompt Flow Integrity), mandatory access control (SEAgent), sandboxed evaluations with real tools (GrantBox), and defense‑in‑depth stacks that gate or isolate dangerous operations; multiple studies report measurable improvements in safety/utility and diagnose critical pitfalls when privileges are not carefully scoped or enforced. <cite id="f1e26834-0">The main security risk we identify in LLM agents is the noncompliance with Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) … LLM agents often connect to privileged tools (e.g., email, cloud storage) and yet operate as a single principal with full access; this monolithic design poses significant security risks</cite> <cite id="f1e26834-4">PFI suggests design principles (compartmentalization, untrusted‑data processing isolation, privilege escalation guardrails) and improves Secure Utility Rate by 28–63% p over ReAct</cite> <cite id="91acffc3-2">Privilege separation designs divide components into privilege levels and isolate planning vs execution or memory, using sandboxing, containers, and access tokens</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-0">LLM‑generated tools may execute untrusted code; prior work therefore runs them in sandboxes (gVisor/Docker) and isolates plugin execution to minimize impact</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-2">Improper privilege usage by agents leads to information leakage and infrastructure damage; GrantBox integrates real tools and finds 84.8% average attack success in crafted privilege scenarios</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-4">SEAgent formalizes privilege escalation as actions exceeding least privilege and enforces MAC policies with negligible overhead while blocking escalations</cite>.

Mechanisms that use privileges to improve safety and security
- Least‑privilege and privilege separation for agents. Recent frameworks explicitly bring PoLP into the LLM‑agent stack by compartmentalizing components, isolating untrusted data processing, and adding privilege escalation guardrails. Prompt Flow Integrity (PFI) formalizes these principles and reports substantial gains in secure utility versus ReAct on downstream tasks. <cite id="f1e26834-0">PoLP limits a principal’s privilege to the minimum and is enforced by compartmentalization; LLM agents lack such policies and may call privileged tools at any time, enabling attacker data to reach the model</cite> <cite id="f1e26834-4">PFI isolates trusted/untrusted components, guards against escalation, and improves Secure Utility Rate by 28–63% over ReAct</cite>. Surveys of the agentic landscape generalize this into two separation axes: vertical (hierarchical privilege levels, e.g., planner vs executor) and horizontal (parallel components with equal privilege but scoped access), and show how sandboxing, containers, and access tokens instantiate least‑privilege for web, file systems, and databases. <cite id="91acffc3-2">Vertical separation isolates tool‑call planning (high privilege) from result processing (low privilege) and memory minimization; horizontal separation restricts per‑agent scope; agents can separate external environments via sandboxing/containerization/access tokens</cite> <cite id="91acffc3-4">Agents should operate with minimum necessary permissions; privilege separation and identity management define access scopes</cite>.

- Mandatory access control and dynamic policy enforcement. SEAgent models agent systems as an information‑flow graph and enforces attribute‑based policies to monitor and block over‑privileged tool calls and confused‑deputy–like attacks in multi‑agent settings. <cite id="3d22351b-4">SEAgent formalizes privilege escalation as exceeding least privilege, identifies novel escalation scenarios including confused deputy variants, and blocks escalations with low false positives and negligible overhead</cite>. Complementary systems like GoEX validate actions post‑facto and isolate dangerous operations via sandboxing, while ACE decouples planning from execution against untrusted third‑party apps to reduce blast radius. <cite id="91acffc3-3">GoEX isolates dangerous operations through sandboxing and performs post‑facto validation; ACE decouples planning into two phases to defend against untrusted third‑party apps; these can be layered in defense‑in‑depth with other prompt‑injection defenses</cite>.

- Capability gating, isolation, and defense‑in‑depth for tools and plugins. Beyond static ACLs, prior work gates and isolates capabilities at the tool/plugin level, runs code in containers, and evaluates interactions under prompt‑injection stress. <cite id="3d22351b-0">Sandboxing is used to execute untrusted code from LLM tools (gVisor/Docker) and to run each OpenAI plugin in a separate sandbox, minimizing impact</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-2">GrantBox automatically integrates real tools, evaluates privilege usage under prompt injection, and finds agents vulnerable with 84.8% average attack success in crafted scenarios</cite>. Surveys catalog a defense stack that mixes privilege/type separation, identity management, and input‑source separation to mitigate interference and prompt injection, noting that many defenses can be composed for stronger coverage. <cite id="91acffc3-3">Several systems implement privilege/type separation for inputs, information‑flow control to prevent prompt injection and privacy leakage, post‑facto validation and sandboxing, and phased planning to defend third‑party apps; taken together, they form defense‑in‑depth</cite>.

- Safe use of real‑world tools and environment privileges. Empirical systems like GrantBox stress‑test whether least‑privilege holds when agents use real MCP servers and tools, revealing high attack success without strong privilege controls and motivating runtime gating, monitoring, and isolation. <cite id="3d22351b-2">GrantBox integrates real tools and shows that despite basic awareness, agents remain vulnerable to sophisticated attacks with 84.8% average attack success</cite>. Broader evaluations of agentic privilege usage echo that productivity gains from real tools come with transferred privileges that must be constrained to avoid leakage and damage. <cite id="f1e26834-1">Equipping agents with real‑world tools transfers privileges to the agent and underlying LLM; improper use can cause leakage and infrastructure damage, motivating privilege control</cite>.

Evaluations, metrics, and trade‑offs
- Measured safety/utility improvements. PFI reports a 28–63% point increase in Secure Utility Rate over ReAct after enforcing least‑privilege guardrails such as compartmentalization and escalation controls. <cite id="f1e26834-4">PFI improves Secure Utility Rate by 28–63% p compared to ReAct by enforcing privilege‑escalation guardrails and component isolation</cite>. SEAgent demonstrates that policy enforcement can block diverse privilege‑escalation vectors with low false positives and negligible overhead, supporting practical deployability. <cite id="3d22351b-4">SEAgent blocks various privilege escalations with low false positive rate and negligible system overhead</cite>.

- High risk when privileges are unscoped. Sandboxed evaluations with real tools show that, absent strict controls, attackers can often hijack agent behavior via prompt injection or over‑privileged operations, achieving high success rates. <cite id="3d22351b-2">Agents remain vulnerable to sophisticated attacks with 84.8% average attack success when evaluated with real tools under prompt injection</cite>. Red‑team analyses of popular agentic stacks frequently find least‑privilege violations (e.g., containers with unnecessary capabilities, exposing host APIs or docker sockets), enabling sandbox escapes and lateral moves. <cite id="3d22351b-1">Attacker code can move from worker to orchestrator and execute on the host if APIs are unauthenticated; many agents grant more permissions than necessary (e.g., mount docker socket), nullifying sandbox separation</cite>.

- Utility loss from separation. Surveys emphasize that privilege separation may reduce utility by splitting functionality and communication overhead across components; designing effective least‑privilege decompositions and efficient inter‑component communication remains an open challenge. <cite id="91acffc3-2">Dividing functionality into least‑privilege components causes utility loss; efficient communication across isolations is an open challenge</cite>.

Practical patterns and pitfalls
- Design patterns. Several reproducible patterns recur in secure agent design:
  - Compartmentalize planning vs execution and separate memory spaces to bound blast radius. <cite id="91acffc3-2">Planner–executor separation and memory minimization reduce risk</cite>.
  - Enforce identity and scoped tokens for tools and environments, leveraging containers/sandboxes for untrusted code and per‑tool isolation. <cite id="91acffc3-2">Agents can enforce least‑privilege by sandboxing, containerization, and access tokens per environment</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-0">Run untrusted code in gVisor/Docker sandboxes and isolate each plugin in its own sandbox</cite>.
  - Add escalation guardrails and policy monitors (MAC/ABAC) that gate tool actions based on attributes and information‑flow graphs. <cite id="3d22351b-4">SEAgent monitors agent‑tool interactions via an information flow graph and enforces ABAC policies to block privilege escalation</cite>.
  - Layer defenses: input‑source separation, prompt‑injection controls, validators, and post‑facto sandboxed execution. <cite id="91acffc3-3">Systems separate privileges/types for inputs, apply information‑flow control to prevent prompt injection, validate actions via sandboxing, and decouple planning to defend third‑party apps</cite>.
- Common pitfalls. Over‑privileged sandboxes and tooling (e.g., unauthenticated APIs, host‑mounted sockets) undermine containment; red‑teaming shows that convenience configurations often defeat security goals. <cite id="3d22351b-1">Containers are often over‑privileged (e.g., --network=host or docker socket mounts), enabling sandbox escapes; unauthenticated APIs allow direct user message injection to execute code on host</cite>. LLMs’ probabilistic nature complicates guarantees: untrusted data flows into agent context and can influence tool usage unless strictly compartmentalized. <cite id="f1e26834-0">At each inference step, agents supply full context (including untrusted data) to the model; without compartmentalization and least privilege, attacker data via connected tools can reach the agent</cite>.

What’s still open and how to build on these ideas
- Granular privilege modeling and dynamic revocation. While many systems define static roles or per‑tool permissions, dynamic risk assessment and runtime privilege revocation tailored to agent states remain underexplored; surveys note that composing defenses and maintaining utility without excessive isolation is an open problem. <cite id="91acffc3-2">Dividing into effective least‑privilege components and reducing communication overhead is an open challenge; current work often addresses generic prompt injection in simplified environments</cite>.
- Real‑world robustness. Benchmarks that integrate real tools and environments reveal high attack success without strict controls; progress will likely require stronger runtime monitors, adaptive escalation policies, and continuous privilege audit logging. <cite id="3d22351b-2">Agents show basic awareness but 84.8% average attack success in crafted privilege‑sensitive scenarios</cite>.
- Composability and ergonomics. Defense‑in‑depth stacks can be composed (gating + isolation + validators + identity controls), but toolchains must be ergonomic for developers and maintain agent productivity. <cite id="91acffc3-3">Multiple approaches can be combined for defense‑in‑depth, trading some utility for security and preventing cross‑domain exploitation</cite>.

Practical takeaways
- If you want “more secure/safe” agents today, adopt least‑privilege by design: compartmentalize planner/executor and memory, gate tool calls with attribute‑based or information‑flow policies, and execute untrusted tool code in isolated sandboxes with minimal capabilities. <cite id="f1e26834-0">LLM agents often connect to privileged tools and lack compartmentalization; enforcing PoLP and isolating untrusted data is essential</cite> <cite id="91acffc3-2">Vertical/horizontal privilege separation with sandboxing and token scoping reduces risk</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-4">MAC/ABAC monitoring can block escalations with low overhead</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-0">Run untrusted code and each plugin in its own sandbox</cite>.
- Validate end‑to‑end with real tools; measure secure utility and attack success under prompt injection. <cite id="3d22351b-2">GrantBox shows realistic evaluation with real tools and quantifies vulnerability; secure utility can be improved with PFI‑style guardrails</cite>.
- Avoid over‑privileged sandboxes and exposed APIs; harden container policies and untrusted tool integrations. <cite id="3d22351b-1">Over‑privileged containers and unauthenticated APIs enable sandbox escape and host execution</cite>.

In short, yes—there are clear prior works that “use privileges” (least privilege, separation, and access control) to make LLMs and LLM agents safer, with both principled frameworks and empirical defenses; the main trade‑off is utility loss from isolation, but recent systems show that principled privilege control can substantially improve safety while preserving usable performance. <cite id="f1e26834-4">Enforcing privilege escalation guardrails and compartmentalization yields 28–63% p improvements in secure utility over strong baselines</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-2">Yet, in realistic settings without strict controls, average attack success can reach 84.8%, underscoring the need for privilege‑aware design and evaluation</cite>.

Title: Prompt Flow Integrity to Prevent Privilege Escalation in LLM Agents
Snippet: The main security risk we identify in LLM agents is the noncompliance with Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) [46]. PoLP is a security principle that limits a principal's privilege to the minimum. It is commonly enforced by compartmentalization [31], which isolates principals into distinct protection domains (e.g., processes, sandboxes). Each protection domain is granted access only to the minimum set of resources and operations for its intended purpose. In general-purpose software systems, the minimum privilege is typically defined by the trust level of a principal. For instance, in operating systems, untrusted user processes are granted a restricted set of privileges when accessing kernel resources and operations. Similarly, in web browsers, the Rule Of 2 [24] ensures that no more than two of the following conditions are simultaneously satisfied: (i) untrusted data, (ii) unsafe implementation, and (iii) high privilege. 

As a new principal in the LLM-powered computing  paradigm [49], LLM agents lack both compartmentalization and least-privilege policies. To assist users with personalized tasks, LLM agents are often connected to privileged tools that grant access to private user data (e.g., email, cloud storage, and file system). Despite the diverse privileges these tools entail, current LLM agents by default operate as a single principal with full access over all tools and data; an agent can call any tool at any time, even when the agent is potentially controlled by the attacker. This monolithic design poses significant security risks. As tools bridge LLM agents and external systems, various data from external data flow into the agent, including untrusted data from attackers. Attackers can inject data into the agent by poisoning the external systems connected with tools (e.g., web search index, email). To prevent attackers from illegally accessing user's private data, the impact of untrusted data should be carefully controlled. 

However, a such security guarantee is difficult to achieve due to the probabilistic nature of LLMs. At each LLM inference step, the LLM agent supplies the entire context, including untrusted data, to the LLM.
</snippet>
<snippet id=f1e26834-1>
Title: Evaluating Privilege Usage of Agents with Real-World Tools
Snippet: Equipping LLM agents with real-world tools can substantially improve productivity. However, granting agents autonomy over tool use also transfers the associated privileges to both the agent and the underlying LLM. Improper privilege usage may lead to serious consequences, including information leakage and infrastructure damage. While several benchmarks have been built to study agents' security, they often rely on pre-coded tools and restricted interaction patterns. Such crafted environments differ substantially from the real-world, making it hard to assess agents' security capabilities in critical privilege control and usage. Therefore, we propose GrantBox, a security evaluation sandbox for analyzing agent privilege usage. GrantBox automatically integrates real-world tools and allows LLM agents to invoke genuine privileges, enabling the evaluation of privilege usage under prompt injection attacks. Our results indicate that while LLMs exhibit basic security awareness and can block some direct attacks, they remain vulnerable to more sophisticated attacks, resulting in an average attack success rate of 84.80% in carefully crafted scenarios.
</snippet>

Title: The Attack and Defense Landscape of Agentic AI: A Comprehensive Survey
Snippet: Following the principle of least privilege, traditional security enforces privilege separation by assigning different privilege levels to different software components, exemplified by earlier automation attempts [18]. In agents, this concept extends to assigning privileges to different components and isolating these components to minimize the overall risk to the system. Design Dimensions. Privilege separation designs vary by separation policy and scope. 

A separation policy can be designed in vertical and horizontal directions. Vertical separation divides components into hierarchical privilege levels, where higher-privilege components (e.g., trusted planners) have more authority than lower-privilege components (e.g., untrusted data processors). Similar to kernel-user separation in operating systems, planner-processor separation designs [5,28,31,67,79,166,168] isolate tool call planning (high privilege) from tool result processing (low privilege). Memory minimization [11] separates the data minimizer (high privilege) from the untrusted data processing unit (low privilege). Horizontal separation partitions the system into parallel components with equal privileges but isolated access scopes. For example, per-application or per-functionality agents [78,170] each interact only with their dedicated tools and resources, preventing cross-domain exploitation. 

The scope of privilege separation indicates the component being separated. An LLM can be separated into planning tool calls and processing results [28,31,67,168], preventing tool results from directly influencing planning decisions. Memory separation [11] creates separate memory spaces, protecting sensitive data from lower-privilege components. Agents can separate external environments to enforce least-privilege [67,78,170], leveraging sandboxing, containerization [84-86], and access tokens [52,145]. 

Limitations and Open Challenges. Current privilege separation research primarily addresses generic indirect prompt injection in simplified environments [32]. It often fails to address real-world environment risks that present diverse and complex challenges requiring specialized separation strategies, such as web, file systems, and databases. Privilege separation entails utility loss by splitting functionality across isolated components. Dividing an agent into an effective set of least-privilege components remains an open challenge. Designing efficient communication across isolated components to reduce utility loss while maintaining security guarantees presents ongoing challenges for practical deployment.
</snippet>

Title: SandboxEval: Towards Securing Test Environment for Untrusted Code
Snippet: Due to the risk of LLM-based tools generating untrusted code, several research studies have highlighted the importance of setting up a sandbox that executes code in an isolated environment to mitigate the potential risks of running untrusted code on the host system [2,6,43,21]. 

Utilize Sandboxing. Chen et al. [2] noted that publicly available programs and model-generated programs may have unknown intent [13], and executing these programs poses a security risk. Therefore, they developed a sandbox environment using gVisor container to safely run untrusted programs against unit tests in their experiments. Siddiq et al. [44] also tested whether the LLM-generated code had any security issues using unit tests. To do this, they utilized a Dockerbased testing environment to execute the code in a sandbox, preventing unsafe behavior. For a similar reason, Du et al. [21] and Sun et al. [45] adopted a sandbox to execute code in an isolated environment to reduce the risk of running untrusted code from unverified sources. 

Build Sandboxing. Given the accessibility of agents for automated execution or installation, there is a significant risk associated with failing to operate LLM agents in a controlled environment. Therefore, Ruan et al. [46] proposed a framework that uses one LLM as an emulator and another as an evaluator in a safety assessment to mitigate the risks posed by LLM agents. Similarly, Wu et al. [47] proposed an execution isolation architecture for LLM-based systems to mitigate security and privacy issues that arise from executing third-party applications within systems. Additionally, because setting up the environment for each test scenario manually and identifying risky cases is challenging, LLM agents have recently been used to complete tasks in a simulated environment [48,49,16]. Moreover, Iqbal et al. [50] run each OpenAI plugin in a different sandbox to minimize the impact of a problematic plugin. In contrast, Mushsharat et al. [51] defined a neural sandbox framework for classification tasks based on similarity between model responses and predefined definitions.

Title: Red-Teaming the Agentic Red-Team
Snippet: A good example of the latter case is a sandbox escape on AIRecon. Its worker container is granted --network=host (among others), allowing an attacker with code execution on the worker to reach the host's network. The orchestrator, running on the host, exposes unauthenticated APIs used to manage agent execution and prompting (/api/chat), allowing an attacker to submit user messages directly to the LLM. One of the tools available to the agent is python_session, which, given a string of Python code, will execute it. However, execution is not performed on the worker but on the orchestrator, i.e., as a host process. To achieve code execution on the host, the attacker invokes /api/chat from the worker, instructing the LLM to call python_session with attacker-controlled code, which will be executed on the host machine. Since the request arrives as a user message (i.e., mimicking an explicit user request rather than an injection in a tool result) the LLM executes it without scrutiny. 

In general, the careful and secure granting of such capabilities is not, in itself, the root cause. However, we observe a more general violation of the least-privilege principle, where containers are often provisioned with more permissions than strictly necessary, or are configured to run in fully privileged mode for convenience. For instance, some agents such as CAI and PentAGI mount the docker socket, nullifying the sandbox separation by design. The sandbox escapes we managed to perform on the test agents are detailed in Table A.3 in Appendix A; the agents without an OS-level sandbox (METATRON, nebula, and xalgorix) are omitted, as they grant immediate host access and thus require no escape. 

While there is clearly a functionality-sandboxing trade-off, in § 9.3 we propose a more principled design that enables full functionality while preserving worker containment.
</snippet>

Title: Evaluating Privilege Usage of Agents with Real-World Tools
Snippet: Equipping LLM agents with real-world tools can substantially improve productivity. However, granting agents autonomy over tool use also transfers the associated privileges to both the agent and the underlying LLM. Improper privilege usage may lead to serious consequences, including information leakage and infrastructure damage. While several benchmarks have been built to study agents' security, they often rely on pre-coded tools and restricted interaction patterns. Such crafted environments differ substantially from the real-world, making it hard to assess agents' security capabilities in critical privilege control and usage. Therefore, we propose GrantBox, a security evaluation sandbox for analyzing agent privilege usage. GrantBox automatically integrates real-world tools and allows LLM agents to invoke genuine privileges, enabling the evaluation of privilege usage under prompt injection attacks. Our results indicate that while LLMs exhibit basic security awareness and can block some direct attacks, they remain vulnerable to more sophisticated attacks, resulting in an average attack success rate of 84.80% in carefully crafted scenarios.
</snippet>

Title: Taming Various Privilege Escalation in LLM-Based Agent Systems: A Mandatory Access Control Framework
Snippet: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agent systems are increasingly deployed for complex real-world tasks but remain vulnerable to natural language-based attacks that exploit over-privileged tool use. This paper aims to understand and mitigate such attacks through the lens of privilege escalation, defined as agent actions exceeding the least privilege required for a user's intended task. Based on a formal model of LLM agent systems, we identify novel privilege escalation scenarios, particularly in multi-agent systems, including a variant akin to the classic confused deputy problem. To defend against both known and newly demonstrated privilege escalation, we propose SEAgent, a mandatory access control (MAC) framework built upon attribute-based access control (ABAC). SEAgent monitors agent-tool interactions via an information flow graph and enforces customizable security policies based on entity attributes. Our evaluations show that SEAgent effectively blocks various privilege escalation while maintaining a low false positive rate and negligible system overhead. This demonstrates its robustness and adaptability in securing LLM-based agent systems.

A remaining gap would be highly granular runtime privilege revocation tied to dynamic risk scoring; however, the retrieved “TriageGPT-like” and isolation/validator works cover strong baselines. I will synthesize into an answer with sections: (1) Short answer, (2) Mechanisms that use privileges (least privilege, separation, DAC/MAC, gating/validator), (3) Evaluations/metrics and trade-offs, (4) Practical patterns and pitfalls, and (5) What’s still open.

Summary answer
Yes. A growing body of LLM and LLM‑agent research explicitly operationalizes “privilege” through least‑privilege policies, capability isolation, access control, and gated tool use to make agents safer. Representative approaches include principled privilege‑separation frameworks (e.g., Prompt Flow Integrity), mandatory access control (SEAgent), sandboxed evaluations with real tools (GrantBox), and defense‑in‑depth stacks that gate or isolate dangerous operations; multiple studies report measurable improvements in safety/utility and diagnose critical pitfalls when privileges are not carefully scoped or enforced. <cite id="f1e26834-0">The main security risk we identify in LLM agents is the noncompliance with Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) … LLM agents often connect to privileged tools (e.g., email, cloud storage) and yet operate as a single principal with full access; this monolithic design poses significant security risks</cite> <cite id="f1e26834-4">PFI suggests design principles (compartmentalization, untrusted‑data processing isolation, privilege escalation guardrails) and improves Secure Utility Rate by 28–63% p over ReAct</cite> <cite id="91acffc3-2">Privilege separation designs divide components into privilege levels and isolate planning vs execution or memory, using sandboxing, containers, and access tokens</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-0">LLM‑generated tools may execute untrusted code; prior work therefore runs them in sandboxes (gVisor/Docker) and isolates plugin execution to minimize impact</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-2">Improper privilege usage by agents leads to information leakage and infrastructure damage; GrantBox integrates real tools and finds 84.8% average attack success in crafted privilege scenarios</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-4">SEAgent formalizes privilege escalation as actions exceeding least privilege and enforces MAC policies with negligible overhead while blocking escalations</cite>.

Mechanisms that use privileges to improve safety and security
- Least‑privilege and privilege separation for agents. Recent frameworks explicitly bring PoLP into the LLM‑agent stack by compartmentalizing components, isolating untrusted data processing, and adding privilege escalation guardrails. Prompt Flow Integrity (PFI) formalizes these principles and reports substantial gains in secure utility versus ReAct on downstream tasks. <cite id="f1e26834-0">PoLP limits a principal’s privilege to the minimum and is enforced by compartmentalization; LLM agents lack such policies and may call privileged tools at any time, enabling attacker data to reach the model</cite> <cite id="f1e26834-4">PFI isolates trusted/untrusted components, guards against escalation, and improves Secure Utility Rate by 28–63% over ReAct</cite>. Surveys of the agentic landscape generalize this into two separation axes: vertical (hierarchical privilege levels, e.g., planner vs executor) and horizontal (parallel components with equal privilege but scoped access), and show how sandboxing, containers, and access tokens instantiate least‑privilege for web, file systems, and databases. <cite id="91acffc3-2">Vertical separation isolates tool‑call planning (high privilege) from result processing (low privilege) and memory minimization; horizontal separation restricts per‑agent scope; agents can separate external environments via sandboxing/containerization/access tokens</cite> <cite id="91acffc3-4">Agents should operate with minimum necessary permissions; privilege separation and identity management define access scopes</cite>.

- Mandatory access control and dynamic policy enforcement. SEAgent models agent systems as an information‑flow graph and enforces attribute‑based policies to monitor and block over‑privileged tool calls and confused‑deputy–like attacks in multi‑agent settings. <cite id="3d22351b-4">SEAgent formalizes privilege escalation as exceeding least privilege, identifies novel escalation scenarios including confused deputy variants, and blocks escalations with low false positives and negligible overhead</cite>. Complementary systems like GoEX validate actions post‑facto and isolate dangerous operations via sandboxing, while ACE decouples planning from execution against untrusted third‑party apps to reduce blast radius. <cite id="91acffc3-3">GoEX isolates dangerous operations through sandboxing and performs post‑facto validation; ACE decouples planning into two phases to defend against untrusted third‑party apps; these can be layered in defense‑in‑depth with other prompt‑injection defenses</cite>.

- Capability gating, isolation, and defense‑in‑depth for tools and plugins. Beyond static ACLs, prior work gates and isolates capabilities at the tool/plugin level, runs code in containers, and evaluates interactions under prompt‑injection stress. <cite id="3d22351b-0">Sandboxing is used to execute untrusted code from LLM tools (gVisor/Docker) and to run each OpenAI plugin in a separate sandbox, minimizing impact</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-2">GrantBox automatically integrates real tools, evaluates privilege usage under prompt injection, and finds agents vulnerable with 84.8% average attack success in crafted scenarios</cite>. Surveys catalog a defense stack that mixes privilege/type separation, identity management, and input‑source separation to mitigate interference and prompt injection, noting that many defenses can be composed for stronger coverage. <cite id="91acffc3-3">Several systems implement privilege/type separation for inputs, information‑flow control to prevent prompt injection and privacy leakage, post‑facto validation and sandboxing, and phased planning to defend third‑party apps; taken together, they form defense‑in‑depth</cite>.

- Safe use of real‑world tools and environment privileges. Empirical systems like GrantBox stress‑test whether least‑privilege holds when agents use real MCP servers and tools, revealing high attack success without strong privilege controls and motivating runtime gating, monitoring, and isolation. <cite id="3d22351b-2">GrantBox integrates real tools and shows that despite basic awareness, agents remain vulnerable to sophisticated attacks with 84.8% average attack success</cite>. Broader evaluations of agentic privilege usage echo that productivity gains from real tools come with transferred privileges that must be constrained to avoid leakage and damage. <cite id="f1e26834-1">Equipping agents with real‑world tools transfers privileges to the agent and underlying LLM; improper use can cause leakage and infrastructure damage, motivating privilege control</cite>.

Evaluations, metrics, and trade‑offs
- Measured safety/utility improvements. PFI reports a 28–63% point increase in Secure Utility Rate over ReAct after enforcing least‑privilege guardrails such as compartmentalization and escalation controls. <cite id="f1e26834-4">PFI improves Secure Utility Rate by 28–63% p compared to ReAct by enforcing privilege‑escalation guardrails and component isolation</cite>. SEAgent demonstrates that policy enforcement can block diverse privilege‑escalation vectors with low false positives and negligible overhead, supporting practical deployability. <cite id="3d22351b-4">SEAgent blocks various privilege escalations with low false positive rate and negligible system overhead</cite>.

- High risk when privileges are unscoped. Sandboxed evaluations with real tools show that, absent strict controls, attackers can often hijack agent behavior via prompt injection or over‑privileged operations, achieving high success rates. <cite id="3d22351b-2">Agents remain vulnerable to sophisticated attacks with 84.8% average attack success when evaluated with real tools under prompt injection</cite>. Red‑team analyses of popular agentic stacks frequently find least‑privilege violations (e.g., containers with unnecessary capabilities, exposing host APIs or docker sockets), enabling sandbox escapes and lateral moves. <cite id="3d22351b-1">Attacker code can move from worker to orchestrator and execute on the host if APIs are unauthenticated; many agents grant more permissions than necessary (e.g., mount docker socket), nullifying sandbox separation</cite>.

- Utility loss from separation. Surveys emphasize that privilege separation may reduce utility by splitting functionality and communication overhead across components; designing effective least‑privilege decompositions and efficient inter‑component communication remains an open challenge. <cite id="91acffc3-2">Dividing functionality into least‑privilege components causes utility loss; efficient communication across isolations is an open challenge</cite>.

Practical patterns and pitfalls
- Design patterns. Several reproducible patterns recur in secure agent design:
  - Compartmentalize planning vs execution and separate memory spaces to bound blast radius. <cite id="91acffc3-2">Planner–executor separation and memory minimization reduce risk</cite>.
  - Enforce identity and scoped tokens for tools and environments, leveraging containers/sandboxes for untrusted code and per‑tool isolation. <cite id="91acffc3-2">Agents can enforce least‑privilege by sandboxing, containerization, and access tokens per environment</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-0">Run untrusted code in gVisor/Docker sandboxes and isolate each plugin in its own sandbox</cite>.
  - Add escalation guardrails and policy monitors (MAC/ABAC) that gate tool actions based on attributes and information‑flow graphs. <cite id="3d22351b-4">SEAgent monitors agent‑tool interactions via an information flow graph and enforces ABAC policies to block privilege escalation</cite>.
  - Layer defenses: input‑source separation, prompt‑injection controls, validators, and post‑facto sandboxed execution. <cite id="91acffc3-3">Systems separate privileges/types for inputs, apply information‑flow control to prevent prompt injection, validate actions via sandboxing, and decouple planning to defend third‑party apps</cite>.
- Common pitfalls. Over‑privileged sandboxes and tooling (e.g., unauthenticated APIs, host‑mounted sockets) undermine containment; red‑teaming shows that convenience configurations often defeat security goals. <cite id="3d22351b-1">Containers are often over‑privileged (e.g., --network=host or docker socket mounts), enabling sandbox escapes; unauthenticated APIs allow direct user message injection to execute code on host</cite>. LLMs’ probabilistic nature complicates guarantees: untrusted data flows into agent context and can influence tool usage unless strictly compartmentalized. <cite id="f1e26834-0">At each inference step, agents supply full context (including untrusted data) to the model; without compartmentalization and least privilege, attacker data via connected tools can reach the agent</cite>.

What’s still open and how to build on these ideas
- Granular privilege modeling and dynamic revocation. While many systems define static roles or per‑tool permissions, dynamic risk assessment and runtime privilege revocation tailored to agent states remain underexplored; surveys note that composing defenses and maintaining utility without excessive isolation is an open problem. <cite id="91acffc3-2">Dividing into effective least‑privilege components and reducing communication overhead is an open challenge; current work often addresses generic prompt injection in simplified environments</cite>.
- Real‑world robustness. Benchmarks that integrate real tools and environments reveal high attack success without strict controls; progress will likely require stronger runtime monitors, adaptive escalation policies, and continuous privilege audit logging. <cite id="3d22351b-2">Agents show basic awareness but 84.8% average attack success in crafted privilege‑sensitive scenarios</cite>.
- Composability and ergonomics. Defense‑in‑depth stacks can be composed (gating + isolation + validators + identity controls), but toolchains must be ergonomic for developers and maintain agent productivity. <cite id="91acffc3-3">Multiple approaches can be combined for defense‑in‑depth, trading some utility for security and preventing cross‑domain exploitation</cite>.

Practical takeaways
- If you want “more secure/safe” agents today, adopt least‑privilege by design: compartmentalize planner/executor and memory, gate tool calls with attribute‑based or information‑flow policies, and execute untrusted tool code in isolated sandboxes with minimal capabilities. <cite id="f1e26834-0">LLM agents often connect to privileged tools and lack compartmentalization; enforcing PoLP and isolating untrusted data is essential</cite> <cite id="91acffc3-2">Vertical/horizontal privilege separation with sandboxing and token scoping reduces risk</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-4">MAC/ABAC monitoring can block escalations with low overhead</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-0">Run untrusted code and each plugin in its own sandbox</cite>.
- Validate end‑to‑end with real tools; measure secure utility and attack success under prompt injection. <cite id="3d22351b-2">GrantBox shows realistic evaluation with real tools and quantifies vulnerability; secure utility can be improved with PFI‑style guardrails</cite>.
- Avoid over‑privileged sandboxes and exposed APIs; harden container policies and untrusted tool integrations. <cite id="3d22351b-1">Over‑privileged containers and unauthenticated APIs enable sandbox escape and host execution</cite>.

In short, yes—there are clear prior works that “use privileges” (least privilege, separation, and access control) to make LLMs and LLM agents safer, with both principled frameworks and empirical defenses; the main trade‑off is utility loss from isolation, but recent systems show that principled privilege control can substantially improve safety while preserving usable performance. <cite id="f1e26834-4">Enforcing privilege escalation guardrails and compartmentalization yields 28–63% p improvements in secure utility over strong baselines</cite> <cite id="3d22351b-2">Yet, in realistic settings without strict controls, average attack success can reach 84.8%, underscoring the need for privilege‑aware design and evaluation</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Prompt Flow Integrity to Prevent Privilege Escalation in LLM Agents
Snippet: The main security risk we identify in LLM agents is the noncompliance with Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) [46]. PoLP is a security principle that limits a principal's privilege to the minimum. It is commonly enforced by compartmentalization [31], which isolates principals into distinct protection domains (e.g., processes, sandboxes). Each protection domain is granted access only to the minimum set of resources and operations for its intended purpose. In general-purpose software systems, the minimum privilege is typically defined by the trust level of a principal. For instance, in operating systems, untrusted user processes are granted a restricted set of privileges when accessing kernel resources and operations. Similarly, in web browsers, the Rule Of 2 [24] ensures that no more than two of the following conditions are simultaneously satisfied: (i) untrusted data, (ii) unsafe implementation, and (iii) high privilege. 

As a new principal in the LLM-powered computing  paradigm [49], LLM agents lack both compartmentalization and least-privilege policies. To assist users with personalized tasks, LLM agents are often connected to privileged tools that grant access to private user data (e.g., email, cloud storage, and file system). Despite the diverse privileges these tools entail, current LLM agents by default operate as a single principal with full access over all tools and data; an agent can call any tool at any time, even when the agent is potentially controlled by the attacker. This monolithic design poses significant security risks. As tools bridge LLM agents and external systems, various data from external data flow into the agent, including untrusted data from attackers. Attackers can inject data into the agent by poisoning the external systems connected with tools (e.g., web search index, email). To prevent attackers from illegally accessing user's private data, the impact of untrusted data should be carefully controlled. 

However, a such security guarantee is difficult to achieve due to the probabilistic nature of LLMs. At each LLM inference step, the LLM agent supplies the entire context, including untrusted data, to the LLM.

Title: SandboxEval: Towards Securing Test Environment for Untrusted Code
Snippet: Due to the risk of LLM-based tools generating untrusted code, several research studies have highlighted the importance of setting up a sandbox that executes code in an isolated environment to mitigate the potential risks of running untrusted code on the host system [2,6,43,21]. 

Utilize Sandboxing. Chen et al. [2] noted that publicly available programs and model-generated programs may have unknown intent [13], and executing these programs poses a security risk. Therefore, they developed a sandbox environment using gVisor container to safely run untrusted programs against unit tests in their experiments. Siddiq et al. [44] also tested whether the LLM-generated code had any security issues using unit tests. To do this, they utilized a Dockerbased testing environment to execute the code in a sandbox, preventing unsafe behavior. For a similar reason, Du et al. [21] and Sun et al. [45] adopted a sandbox to execute code in an isolated environment to reduce the risk of running untrusted code from unverified sources. 

Build Sandboxing. Given the accessibility of agents for automated execution or installation, there is a significant risk associated with failing to operate LLM agents in a controlled environment. Therefore, Ruan et al. [46] proposed a framework that uses one LLM as an emulator and another as an evaluator in a safety assessment to mitigate the risks posed by LLM agents. Similarly, Wu et al. [47] proposed an execution isolation architecture for LLM-based systems to mitigate security and privacy issues that arise from executing third-party applications within systems. Additionally, because setting up the environment for each test scenario manually and identifying risky cases is challenging, LLM agents have recently been used to complete tasks in a simulated environment [48,49,16]. Moreover, Iqbal et al. [50] run each OpenAI plugin in a different sandbox to minimize the impact of a problematic plugin. In contrast, Mushsharat et al. [51] defined a neural sandbox framework for classification tasks based on similarity between model responses and predefined definitions. 

Evaluate Sandboxing.

Title: Red-Teaming the Agentic Red-Team
Snippet: A good example of the latter case is a sandbox escape on AIRecon. Its worker container is granted --network=host (among others), allowing an attacker with code execution on the worker to reach the host's network. The orchestrator, running on the host, exposes unauthenticated APIs used to manage agent execution and prompting (/api/chat), allowing an attacker to submit user messages directly to the LLM. One of the tools available to the agent is python_session, which, given a string of Python code, will execute it. However, execution is not performed on the worker but on the orchestrator, i.e., as a host process. To achieve code execution on the host, the attacker invokes /api/chat from the worker, instructing the LLM to call python_session with attacker-controlled code, which will be executed on the host machine. Since the request arrives as a user message (i.e., mimicking an explicit user request rather than an injection in a tool result) the LLM executes it without scrutiny. 

In general, the careful and secure granting of such capabilities is not, in itself, the root cause. However, we observe a more general violation of the least-privilege principle, where containers are often provisioned with more permissions than strictly necessary, or are configured to run in fully privileged mode for convenience. For instance, some agents such as CAI and PentAGI mount the docker socket, nullifying the sandbox separation by design. The sandbox escapes we managed to perform on the test agents are detailed in Table A.3 in Appendix A; the agents without an OS-level sandbox (METATRON, nebula, and xalgorix) are omitted, as they grant immediate host access and thus require no escape. 

While there is clearly a functionality-sandboxing trade-off, in § 9.3 we propose a more principled design that enables full functionality while preserving worker containment.

Title: Evaluating Privilege Usage of Agents with Real-World Tools
Snippet: Equipping LLM agents with real-world tools can substantially improve productivity. However, granting agents autonomy over tool use also transfers the associated privileges to both the agent and the underlying LLM. Improper privilege usage may lead to serious consequences, including information leakage and infrastructure damage. While several benchmarks have been built to study agents' security, they often rely on pre-coded tools and restricted interaction patterns. Such crafted environments differ substantially from the real-world, making it hard to assess agents' security capabilities in critical privilege control and usage. Therefore, we propose GrantBox, a security evaluation sandbox for analyzing agent privilege usage. GrantBox automatically integrates real-world tools and allows LLM agents to invoke genuine privileges, enabling the evaluation of privilege usage under prompt injection attacks. Our results indicate that while LLMs exhibit basic security awareness and can block some direct attacks, they remain vulnerable to more sophisticated attacks, resulting in an average attack success rate of 84.80% in carefully crafted scenarios.

Title: Prompt Flow Integrity to Prevent Privilege Escalation in LLM Agents

Title: Taming Various Privilege Escalation in LLM-Based Agent Systems: A Mandatory Access Control Framework
Snippet: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agent systems are increasingly deployed for complex real-world tasks but remain vulnerable to natural language-based attacks that exploit over-privileged tool use. This paper aims to understand and mitigate such attacks through the lens of privilege escalation, defined as agent actions exceeding the least privilege required for a user's intended task. Based on a formal model of LLM agent systems, we identify novel privilege escalation scenarios, particularly in multi-agent systems, including a variant akin to the classic confused deputy problem. To defend against both known and newly demonstrated privilege escalation, we propose SEAgent, a mandatory access control (MAC) framework built upon attribute-based access control (ABAC). SEAgent monitors agent-tool interactions via an information flow graph and enforces customizable security policies based on entity attributes. Our evaluations show that SEAgent effectively blocks various privilege escalation while maintaining a low false positive rate and negligible system overhead. This demonstrates its robustness and adaptability in securing LLM-based agent systems.

To achieve code execution on the host, the attacker invokes /api/chat from the worker, instructing the LLM to call python_session with attacker-controlled code, which will be executed on the host machine. Since the request arrives as a user message (i.e., mimicking an explicit user request rather than an injection in a tool result) the LLM executes it without scrutiny. 

In general, the careful and secure granting of such capabilities is not, in itself, the root cause. However, we observe a more general violation of the least-privilege principle, where containers are often provisioned with more permissions than strictly necessary, or are configured to run in fully privileged mode for convenience. For instance, some agents such as CAI and PentAGI mount the docker socket, nullifying the sandbox separation by design. The sandbox escapes we managed to perform on the test agents are detailed in Table A.3 in Appendix A; the agents without an OS-level sandbox (METATRON, nebula, and xalgorix) are omitted, as they grant immediate host access and thus require no escape. 

While there is clearly a functionality-sandboxing trade-off, in § 9.3 we propose a more principled design that enables full functionality while preserving worker containment.

documents.title: Evaluating Privilege Usage of Agents with Real-World Tools
documents.snippet: Equipping LLM agents with real-world tools can substantially improve productivity. However, granting agents autonomy over tool use also transfers the associated privileges to both the agent and the underlying LLM. Improper privilege usage may lead to serious consequences, including information leakage and infrastructure damage. While several benchmarks have been built to study agents' security, they often rely on pre-coded tools and restricted interaction patterns. Such crafted environments differ substantially from the real-world, making it hard to assess agents' security capabilities in critical privilege control and usage. Therefore, we propose GrantBox, a security evaluation sandbox for analyzing agent privilege usage. GrantBox automatically integrates real-world tools and allows LLM agents to invoke genuine privileges, enabling the evaluation of privilege usage under prompt injection attacks. Our results indicate that while LLMs exhibit basic security awareness and can block some direct attacks, they remain vulnerable to more sophisticated attacks, resulting in an average attack success rate of 84.80% in carefully crafted scenarios.

documents.title: Prompt Flow Integrity to Prevent Privilege Escalation in LLM Agents
Taming Various Privilege Escalation in LLM-Based Agent Systems: A Mandatory Access Control Framework
documents.snippet: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agent systems are increasingly deployed for complex real-world tasks but remain vulnerable to natural language-based attacks that exploit over-privileged tool use. This paper aims to understand and mitigate such attacks through the lens of privilege escalation, defined as agent actions exceeding the least privilege required for a user's intended task. Based on a formal model of LLM agent systems, we identify novel privilege escalation scenarios, particularly in multi-agent systems, including a variant akin to the classic confused deputy problem. To defend against both known and newly demonstrated privilege escalation, we propose SEAgent, a mandatory access control (MAC) framework built upon attribute-based access control (ABAC). SEAgent monitors agent-tool interactions via an information flow graph and enforces customizable security policies based on entity attributes. Our evaluations show that SEAgent effectively blocks various privilege escalation while maintaining a low false positive rate and negligible system overhead. This demonstrates its robustness and adaptability in securing LLM-based agent systems.

Summary answer
Existing LLM agent privilege mechanisms do not demonstrate the Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) with strong, principled enforcement, i.e., they do not compartmentalize authority so that each component operates with only the minimum necessary privileges and isolation between trust domains. Agents commonly run as a single monolithic principal with full tool access, rely on coarse “capability gating” without per‑call mediation, and process mixed trusted/untrusted contexts, enabling prompt‑injection–driven privilege escalation and confused‑deputy misuse; these issues have high empirical attack success rates in realistic evaluations. <cite id="ed9b325f-3">As new principals in the LLM‑powered paradigm, LLM agents lack both compartmentalization and least‑privilege policies, often connecting to privileged tools while operating by default as a single principal with full access over all tools and data</cite> <cite id="ed9b325f-2">Enforcing PoLP in LLM agents is inherently challenging because the model processes entire agent contexts and, once untrusted data is injected, attacker data becomes a malicious prompt that instructs actions leading to privilege escalation</cite> <cite id="ed9b325f-0">A security evaluation integrating real MCP servers and tools shows current LLMs remain vulnerable to privilege misuse, especially under prompt injection</cite> <cite id="ed9b325f-1">An average attack success rate of 84.80% was observed for carefully crafted privilege‑sensitive scenarios, despite basic awareness and defenses against some direct attacks</cite>.

Why PoLP/compartmentalization fails today
- Monolithic authority and mixed-context processing: <cite id="ed9b325f-3">Agents connect to privileged tools yet default to one principal that can call any tool at any time, even when potentially controlled by an attacker</cite>. <cite id="87050a50-0">LLM agents manage diverse inputs (trusted prompts, untrusted tool observations, and supply‑chain data) in a single context memory; prompt injection arises from lack of privilege isolation between different trust levels’ inputs, with untrusted inputs mimicking trusted prompts to hijack control flow and escalate privileges</cite>. 
- Absent per‑call mediation and confused‑deputy delegation: <cite id="7717e9ee-0">Even when capability gating limits which tools are exposed, per‑call authorization is often absent: a compromised model can emit a tool call and well‑typed arguments that the runtime accepts as sufficient authority, turning the model into a confused deputy that misuses its authority</cite>. <cite id="7717e9ee-1">Classical systems security emphasizes complete mediation and that confused deputies arise when authority and designation are conflated; the paper audits a default gap “capability gating shipped, per‑call authorization absent,” and proposes a deployable fail‑closed control</cite>. 
- Probabilistic model behavior undermines static separation: <cite id="ed9b325f-2">Due to their probabilistic nature, LLMs process trusted and untrusted data together, allowing injected data to dynamically influence privileged tool usage; malicious prompts or data can directly command tool calls or steer behavior via attention to achieve privilege escalation</cite>. <cite id="ed9b325f-4">Analyses show attacks like indirect prompt injection and memory poisoning often succeed due to insufficient privilege control, motivating system‑level privilege control yet revealing over‑privileged tool selection when lower‑privilege alternatives suffice</cite>.

Related traditional properties not adequately satisfied
- Separation of duty and privilege separation: <cite id="87050a50-0">Prompt injection exploits the single‑context design where different trust levels coexist without privilege isolation</cite>. <cite id="7717e9ee-3">In multi‑agent workflows, delegating full inherited authority to downstream agents violates least privilege; designing bounded, auditable authority with no privilege accumulation and revocable delegation remains unsolved in deployed systems, with confused‑deputy failures specifically identified in multi‑agent LLM systems</cite>. <cite id="7717e9ee-4">Surveys of agentic AI describe vertical and horizontal privilege separation (e.g., isolating planners from processors, data minimizers from untrusted processors, per‑application agents with isolated scopes, and sandboxing/tokens), but note limitations: current separation largely addresses generic prompt injection in simplified environments and suffers utility loss and open challenges in real‑world environments like web, filesystems, and databases</cite>.
- Confidentiality/integrity boundaries and subject–object control: <cite id="87050a50-1">In traditional formal models, Bell–LaPadula addresses confidentiality but does not guarantee integrity, while Biba enforces integrity properties like “don’t read down” and “don’t write up,” yet lacks support for authorization revocation</cite>. <cite id="87050a50-3">Bell–LaPadula classifies subjects/objects by level to prevent high‑level information flow to low‑level subjects, but practical enforcement depends on combining mandatory and discretionary policies</cite>. For LLM agents, mixed untrusted/untrusted‑derived inputs and dynamic tool invocation complicate enforcing analogous no‑read‑up/no‑write‑down information‑flow and integrity constraints; empirical results show large privilege misuse under injection despite awareness defenses. <cite id="ed9b325f-1">Agents can invoke genuine privileges, and sophisticated scenarios achieve high attack success rates, indicating that containment and awareness alone are insufficient</cite>.
- Auditability and revocation: <cite id="7717e9ee-2">Some systems propose per‑agent privilege groups, access request auditing, and logs of activities and control changes to safeguard against privilege abuse, improving transparency</cite>. <cite id="7717e9ee-3">Authorization propagation work emphasizes bounded, auditable authority and revocation along delegation chains, yet no widely deployed authorization system provides a complete solution today; emerging token‑level mechanisms demonstrate feasibility with microsecond‑level boundary verification and sub‑second revocation, but integration into workflow‑scoped authorization remains the bottleneck</cite>. <cite id="ed9b325f-2">Because LLMs integrate untrusted data into the generation process and probabilistically choose actions, maintaining continuous audit and effective revocation at each tool boundary is difficult in practice</cite>.

What would demonstrate the core property (and what doesn’t)
- Missing pieces vs. superficial controls: <cite id="7717e9ee-1">Capability gates alone are insufficient; per‑call authorization that checks arguments, context, and principal at each tool invocation is required, with a fail‑closed default to block untrusted calls</cite>. <cite id="7717e9ee-3">Each agent’s effective authority should be bounded, non‑accumulative across delegation, necessary‑but‑not‑sufficient to the initiating principal, and revocable at any point</cite>. <cite id="ed9b325f-3">Agents should adopt compartmentalization—distinct protection domains for tool use and data access—with least‑privilege policies, rather than a single monolithic principal</cite>. 
- Evidence of continued failure: <cite id="ed9b325f-1">In realistic MCP‑integrated tests, agents remain vulnerable to prompt injection and privilege misuse despite awareness and some gating, with average attack success near 85% in crafted privilege‑sensitive scenarios</cite> <cite id="ed9b325f-0">Analyses attribute these failures to improper privilege usage, including leakage and infrastructure damage risks, underscoring the need for robust least‑privilege enforcement</cite> <cite id="ed9b325f-4">Studies highlight over‑privileged tool selection and insufficient control, motivating system‑level mitigation yet revealing that lower‑privilege alternatives are often chosen when absent</cite>.

Implications and outlook
- The core gap is principled PoLP with dynamic, per‑action mediation and isolation: <cite id="ed9b325f-3">LLM agents lack compartmentalization and default to full tool access</cite> <cite id="7717e9ee-0">even when capability gates exist, per‑call authorization is absent, enabling confused‑deputy misuse</cite>. <cite id="87050a50-0">Prompt‑injection taxonomies show how mixed‑trust context without privilege isolation enables unauthorized escalation</cite>. 
- Emerging defenses make progress but are not yet ubiquitous or foolproof: <cite id="7717e9ee-1">per‑call authorization with fail‑closed controls</cite> <cite id="7717e9ee-3">token‑level capability tokens with fast boundary checks and revocation</cite> <cite id="87050a50-4">planner–processor and processor–planner separation with sandboxing and tokens</cite> address key failures, yet integration challenges and real‑world environment diversity limit coverage. <cite id="7717e9ee-4">Dividing functionality into least‑privilege components with efficient inter‑component communication remains an open challenge</cite>. 
- Foundational integrity/confidentiality models highlight remaining gaps: <cite id="87050a50-1">Mandatory models like Bell–LaPadula/Biba provide strong isolation properties but struggle with revocation and often require additional mechanisms for authorization</cite>, a tension mirrored in LLM agents where dynamic content and evolving delegation complicate continuous auditing and effective revocation. <cite id="7717e9ee-2">System designs that add auditing and privilege grouping improve transparency but are not yet standard across platforms</cite>.

Bottom line
The core traditional property not currently demonstrated by existing LLM agent privilege mechanisms is the Principle of Least Privilege with strong compartmentalization and complete mediation: agents do not enforce per‑action authorization with isolation between trust domains, enabling prompt‑injection–driven privilege escalation and confused‑deputy misuse with high success rates in realistic settings. <cite id="ed9b325f-3">LLM agents lack compartmentalization and least‑privilege policies and default to a single principal with full tool access</cite> <cite id="7717e9ee-0">per‑call authorization is absent, leaving runtime authority to untrusted outputs</cite> <cite id="87050a50-0">mixed untrusted inputs in a single context bypass privilege isolation, enabling unauthorized escalation</cite> <cite id="ed9b325f-1">empirical evaluations show 84.8% attack success in privilege‑sensitive scenarios</cite>. Addressing this requires per‑call authorization, scoped capabilities with fail‑closed defaults, revocable delegation, and robust audit/containment across all tool boundaries. <cite id="7717e9ee-1">Per‑call authorization and fail‑closed controls mitigate confused deputy risks and enforce least privilege</cite> <cite id="7717e9ee-3">bounded, auditable, non‑accumulative authority with revocation</cite> <cite id="87050a50-4">privilege separation via isolation and tokens</cite>.

Title: Prompt Flow Integrity to Prevent Privilege Escalation in LLM Agents
Snippet: The main security risk we identify in LLM agents is the noncompliance with Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) [46]. PoLP is a security principle that limits a principal's privilege to the minimum. It is commonly enforced by compartmentalization [31], which isolates principals into distinct protection domains (e.g., processes, sandboxes). Each protection domain is granted access only to the minimum set of resources and operations for its intended purpose. In general-purpose software systems, the minimum privilege is typically defined by the trust level of a principal. For instance, in operating systems, untrusted user processes are granted a restricted set of privileges when accessing kernel resources and operations. Similarly, in web browsers, the Rule Of 2 [24] ensures that no more than two of the following conditions are simultaneously satisfied: (i) untrusted data, (ii) unsafe implementation, and (iii) high privilege. 

As a new principal in the LLM-powered computing  paradigm [49], LLM agents lack both compartmentalization and least-privilege policies. To assist users with personalized tasks, LLM agents are often connected to privileged tools that grant access to private user data (e.g., email, cloud storage, and file system). Despite the diverse privileges these tools entail, current LLM agents by default operate as a single principal with full access over all tools and data; an agent can call any tool at any time, even when the agent is potentially controlled by the attacker. This monolithic design poses significant security risks. As tools bridge LLM agents and external systems, various data from external data flow into the agent, including untrusted data from attackers. Attackers can inject data into the agent by poisoning the external systems connected with tools (e.g., web search index, email). To prevent attackers from illegally accessing user's private data, the impact of untrusted data should be carefully controlled. 

However, a such security guarantee is difficult to achieve due to the probabilistic nature of LLMs. At each LLM inference step, the LLM agent supplies the entire context, including untrusted data, to the LLM.

Most works treat these inputs as trusted; however, some threat models account for attack surfaces from the 2 data sources [63,90,91]. Thus, we label these 2 inputs as partially trusted. These inputs have different trust levels and co-exist in a single context memory of the LLM agent to affect its behaviors. 

Principles of prompt injection. The prompt injection vulnerability arises from the lack of privilege isolation between different trust levels' inputs. Despite textual delimiters, the model processes the context as a unified semantic sequence, creating ambiguity where untrusted inputs can mimic trusted input to manipulate the agent's behaviors. This results in attention competition: adversarial payloads manipulate the selfattention mechanism, shifting attention weights away from system prompts toward malicious inputs [29,93]. Furthermore, this leads to unauthorized privilege escalation, enabling the hijacking of the agent's control flow.

Title: IBAC Mathematics and Mechanics: The Case for 'Integer Based Access Control' of Data Security in the Age of AI and AI Automation
Snippet: 3 IBAC Process Dominance -Extending the trusted system's model 

We made the point earlier that moving away from the mathematically sound trusted Bell-LaPadula and Biba models to build access control systems such as ABAC and CapBAC, which lack a solid mathematical foundation, was a mistake. Instead, extending the Bell-LaPadula and Biba mathematics to enhance robustness and introduce flexibility should have been the focus. 

From now on, when we refer to Bell-LaPadula, we refer to Bell-LaPadula including the Biba model as well. 

We outline an approach here to extend Bell-LaPadula based on some mathematical research that was developed in the 1990s (see Hargraves). 

Hargraves makes the point in his master's dissertation that Bell-LaPadula can be made more flexible if both the Subject dominates the Object and the Process dominates the Object. 

This is an interesting philosophical shift. The argument being a Subject can only gain access to an Object by some Process, so why is the Process itself not part of the dominance relation and not part of the Bell-LaPadula trusted system model. 

Hargraves [12] indicates that both the Subject and the Process should dominate the object 

We will show that by adding the additional process constraint to the Bell-LaPadula model, the model becomes much more flexible and addresses the original disadvantages of Bell-LaPadula that led to the development of ABAC and CapBAC. 

We describe the extended Bell-LaPadula model and the associated proof using category theory [7]. Category theory is an abstraction of the predicate logic that enables us to express more efficiently and succinctly the necessary mathematics. 

The key point to the Bell-LaPadula extension is that we introduce one-to-one (bijective) relationship mappings between the "Subject" and a "Process" which enables greater flexibility in the model when accessing "objects". 

So in addition to user as the Subject mapped to the Object, we also have combinations of Subjects and Processes, as tuples mapped to the object. 

For example, ("user1", "printer", "secret") and ("user2", "brief ing_room", "topsecret").

Title: Capability Gates Are Not Authorization: Confused-Deputy Failures in LLM Agent Frameworks
Snippet: LLM agents are increasingly deployed as software components that read untrusted text and then invoke tools with real authority. A support agent may read email and refund payments; a sales agent may update CRM records; a workflow agent may call infrastructure APIs; a payment assistant may generate or modify money-moving requests. 

The core security question is not whether the model can be prompted to behave badly. Indirect prompt injection is already established. The narrower systems question is: when a compromised model emits a tool call, what does the runtime do next? 

This paper studies a specific authorization failure mode: capability gating is present, but per-call authorization is absent. Capability gating answers which tools are exposed to an agent. Per-call authorization answers whether this concrete call, with these argument values, in this principal and session context, is allowed. If a runtime exposes issue_refund and then accepts the model's well-typed amount, destination, or payment_intent as sufficient authority, it has delegated the authorization decision to an untrusted parser. 

That is the classic confused-deputy pattern: a privileged component is induced by attacker-controlled input to misuse its authority [2], [1]. Figure 1 summarizes why the distinction matters operationally: cost-optimized deployment-tier models show materially higher ASR task than flagship models in this measured sweep by mean ASR task (no paired CI for the tier aggregate), although high outliers exist in both groups. Each dot is one measured model, and the short horizontal segments mark tier means. The deployment-tier grouping is an economics/deployment inference over cost-optimized models suitable for high-volume agent traffic, not a claim about any provider's internal production fleet. ASR is the model's attempted unauthorized action under sandboxed tooling, not a breach rate. 

We make the claim deliberately narrow. We do not claim to discover prompt injection, and we do not claim the first least-privilege or per-call authorization design for agents. Prior work such as MiniScope, AgentDojo, InjecAgent, ToolEmu, and WASP already covers adjacent ground [10], [6], [7], [8], [9].
</snippet>

Title: Authorization Propagation in Multi-Agent AI Systems: Identity Governance as Infrastructure
Snippet: When a human principal h initiates a workflow that involves agents a 1 , a 2 , . . . , a n , the system must determine the effective authority at each agent. The naive approach -each agent inherits the initiating human's full authority -violates least privilege. The conservative approach -each agent operates only under its own service identity -may be insufficient to complete the workflow. 

The problem is to define a delegation model where: 

• Each agent's effective authority is bounded and auditable 

• Authority does not accumulate through delegation chains (no privilege escalation) 

• The initiating principal's authorization is necessary but not sufficient for downstream access 

• Delegation can be revoked at any point in the chain 

No widely deployed authorization system provides a complete solution to this in the context of autonomous agent-to-agent delegation. The confused deputy problem -where an agent is tricked into misusing its authority on behalf of an unauthorized principal -is a classical formulation of this failure mode, and has been identified in multi-agent LLM systems specifically [Anonymous, 2026f]. However, emerging work on invocation-bound capability tokens [Prakash, 2026] and postquantum delegation chains [Chen, 2026] demonstrates that the token-level mechanisms are feasible. Prakash [2026] achieves 0.049ms per-boundary verification with append-only attenuation, and Chen [2026] provides Tamarin-verified revocation within one second. What remains is integration into a workflow-scoped authorization architecture.
</snippet>

Title: The Attack and Defense Landscape of Agentic AI: A Comprehensive Survey
Snippet: Following the principle of least privilege, traditional security enforces privilege separation by assigning different privilege levels to different software components, exemplified by earlier automation attempts [18]. In agents, this concept extends to assigning privileges to different components and isolating these components to minimize the overall risk to the system. Design Dimensions. Privilege separation designs vary by separation policy and scope. 

A separation policy can be designed in vertical and horizontal directions. Vertical separation divides components into hierarchical privilege levels, where higher-privilege components (e.g., trusted planners) have more authority than lower-privilege components (e.g., untrusted data processors). Similar to kernel-user separation in operating systems, planner-processor separation designs [5,28,31,67,79,166,168] isolate tool call planning (high privilege) from tool result processing (low privilege). Memory minimization [11] separates the data minimizer (high privilege) from the untrusted data processing unit (low privilege). Horizontal separation partitions the system into parallel components with equal privileges but isolated access scopes. For example, per-application or per-functionality agents [78,170] each interact only with their dedicated tools and resources, preventing cross-domain exploitation. 

The scope of privilege separation indicates the component being separated. An LLM can be separated into planning tool calls and processing results [28,31,67,168], preventing tool results from directly influencing planning decisions. Memory separation [11] creates separate memory spaces, protecting sensitive data from lower-privilege components. Agents can separate external environments to enforce least-privilege [67,78,170], leveraging sandboxing, containerization [84-86], and access tokens [52,145]. 

Limitations and Open Challenges. Current privilege separation research primarily addresses generic indirect prompt injection in simplified environments [32]. It often fails to address real-world environment risks that present diverse and complex challenges requiring specialized separation strategies, such as web, file systems, and databases. Privilege separation entails utility loss by splitting functionality across isolated components. Dividing an agent into an effective set of least-privilege components remains an open challenge. Designing efficient communication across isolated components to reduce utility loss while maintaining security guarantees presents ongoing challenges for practical deployment.
