Summary answer
Existing LLM agent privilege mechanisms do not demonstrate the Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) with strong, principled enforcement, i.e., they do not compartmentalize authority so that each component operates with only the minimum necessary privileges and isolation between trust domains. Agents commonly run as a single monolithic principal with full tool access, rely on coarse “capability gating” without per‑call mediation, and process mixed trusted/untrusted contexts, enabling prompt‑injection–driven privilege escalation and confused‑deputy misuse; these issues have high empirical attack success rates in realistic evaluations. <cite id="ed9b325f-3">As new principals in the LLM‑powered paradigm, LLM agents lack both compartmentalization and least‑privilege policies, often connecting to privileged tools while operating by default as a single principal with full access over all tools and data</cite> <cite id="ed9b325f-2">Enforcing PoLP in LLM agents is inherently challenging because the model processes entire agent contexts and, once untrusted data is injected, attacker data becomes a malicious prompt that instructs actions leading to privilege escalation</cite> <cite id="ed9b325f-0">A security evaluation integrating real MCP servers and tools shows current LLMs remain vulnerable to privilege misuse, especially under prompt injection</cite> <cite id="ed9b325f-1">An average attack success rate of 84.80% was observed for carefully crafted privilege‑sensitive scenarios, despite basic awareness and defenses against some direct attacks</cite>.

Why PoLP/compartmentalization fails today
- Monolithic authority and mixed-context processing: <cite id="ed9b325f-3">Agents connect to privileged tools yet default to one principal that can call any tool at any time, even when potentially controlled by an attacker</cite>. <cite id="87050a50-0">LLM agents manage diverse inputs (trusted prompts, untrusted tool observations, and supply‑chain data) in a single context memory; prompt injection arises from lack of privilege isolation between different trust levels’ inputs, with untrusted inputs mimicking trusted prompts to hijack control flow and escalate privileges</cite>. 
- Absent per‑call mediation and confused‑deputy delegation: <cite id="7717e9ee-0">Even when capability gating limits which tools are exposed, per‑call authorization is often absent: a compromised model can emit a tool call and well‑typed arguments that the runtime accepts as sufficient authority, turning the model into a confused deputy that misuses its authority</cite>. <cite id="7717e9ee-1">Classical systems security emphasizes complete mediation and that confused deputies arise when authority and designation are conflated; the paper audits a default gap “capability gating shipped, per‑call authorization absent,” and proposes a deployable fail‑closed control</cite>. 
- Probabilistic model behavior undermines static separation: <cite id="ed9b325f-2">Due to their probabilistic nature, LLMs process trusted and untrusted data together, allowing injected data to dynamically influence privileged tool usage; malicious prompts or data can directly command tool calls or steer behavior via attention to achieve privilege escalation</cite>. <cite id="ed9b325f-4">Analyses show attacks like indirect prompt injection and memory poisoning often succeed due to insufficient privilege control, motivating system‑level privilege control yet revealing over‑privileged tool selection when lower‑privilege alternatives suffice</cite>.

Related traditional properties not adequately satisfied
- Separation of duty and privilege separation: <cite id="87050a50-0">Prompt injection exploits the single‑context design where different trust levels coexist without privilege isolation</cite>. <cite id="7717e9ee-3">In multi‑agent workflows, delegating full inherited authority to downstream agents violates least privilege; designing bounded, auditable authority with no privilege accumulation and revocable delegation remains unsolved in deployed systems, with confused‑deputy failures specifically identified in multi‑agent LLM systems</cite>. <cite id="7717e9ee-4">Surveys of agentic AI describe vertical and horizontal privilege separation (e.g., isolating planners from processors, data minimizers from untrusted processors, per‑application agents with isolated scopes, and sandboxing/tokens), but note limitations: current separation largely addresses generic prompt injection in simplified environments and suffers utility loss and open challenges in real‑world environments like web, filesystems, and databases</cite>.
- Confidentiality/integrity boundaries and subject–object control: <cite id="87050a50-1">In traditional formal models, Bell–LaPadula addresses confidentiality but does not guarantee integrity, while Biba enforces integrity properties like “don’t read down” and “don’t write up,” yet lacks support for authorization revocation</cite>. <cite id="87050a50-3">Bell–LaPadula classifies subjects/objects by level to prevent high‑level information flow to low‑level subjects, but practical enforcement depends on combining mandatory and discretionary policies</cite>. For LLM agents, mixed untrusted/untrusted‑derived inputs and dynamic tool invocation complicate enforcing analogous no‑read‑up/no‑write‑down information‑flow and integrity constraints; empirical results show large privilege misuse under injection despite awareness defenses. <cite id="ed9b325f-1">Agents can invoke genuine privileges, and sophisticated scenarios achieve high attack success rates, indicating that containment and awareness alone are insufficient</cite>.
- Auditability and revocation: <cite id="7717e9ee-2">Some systems propose per‑agent privilege groups, access request auditing, and logs of activities and control changes to safeguard against privilege abuse, improving transparency</cite>. <cite id="7717e9ee-3">Authorization propagation work emphasizes bounded, auditable authority and revocation along delegation chains, yet no widely deployed authorization system provides a complete solution today; emerging token‑level mechanisms demonstrate feasibility with microsecond‑level boundary verification and sub‑second revocation, but integration into workflow‑scoped authorization remains the bottleneck</cite>. <cite id="ed9b325f-2">Because LLMs integrate untrusted data into the generation process and probabilistically choose actions, maintaining continuous audit and effective revocation at each tool boundary is difficult in practice</cite>.

What would demonstrate the core property (and what doesn’t)
- Missing pieces vs. superficial controls: <cite id="7717e9ee-1">Capability gates alone are insufficient; per‑call authorization that checks arguments, context, and principal at each tool invocation is required, with a fail‑closed default to block untrusted calls</cite>. <cite id="7717e9ee-3">Each agent’s effective authority should be bounded, non‑accumulative across delegation, necessary‑but‑not‑sufficient to the initiating principal, and revocable at any point</cite>. <cite id="ed9b325f-3">Agents should adopt compartmentalization—distinct protection domains for tool use and data access—with least‑privilege policies, rather than a single monolithic principal</cite>. 
- Evidence of continued failure: <cite id="ed9b325f-1">In realistic MCP‑integrated tests, agents remain vulnerable to prompt injection and privilege misuse despite awareness and some gating, with average attack success near 85% in crafted privilege‑sensitive scenarios</cite> <cite id="ed9b325f-0">Analyses attribute these failures to improper privilege usage, including leakage and infrastructure damage risks, underscoring the need for robust least‑privilege enforcement</cite> <cite id="ed9b325f-4">Studies highlight over‑privileged tool selection and insufficient control, motivating system‑level mitigation yet revealing that lower‑privilege alternatives are often chosen when absent</cite>.

Implications and outlook
- The core gap is principled PoLP with dynamic, per‑action mediation and isolation: <cite id="ed9b325f-3">LLM agents lack compartmentalization and default to full tool access</cite> <cite id="7717e9ee-0">even when capability gates exist, per‑call authorization is absent, enabling confused‑deputy misuse</cite>. <cite id="87050a50-0">Prompt‑injection taxonomies show how mixed‑trust context without privilege isolation enables unauthorized escalation</cite>. 
- Emerging defenses make progress but are not yet ubiquitous or foolproof: <cite id="7717e9ee-1">per‑call authorization with fail‑closed controls</cite> <cite id="7717e9ee-3">token‑level capability tokens with fast boundary checks and revocation</cite> <cite id="87050a50-4">planner–processor and processor–planner separation with sandboxing and tokens</cite> address key failures, yet integration challenges and real‑world environment diversity limit coverage. <cite id="7717e9ee-4">Dividing functionality into least‑privilege components with efficient inter‑component communication remains an open challenge</cite>. 
- Foundational integrity/confidentiality models highlight remaining gaps: <cite id="87050a50-1">Mandatory models like Bell–LaPadula/Biba provide strong isolation properties but struggle with revocation and often require additional mechanisms for authorization</cite>, a tension mirrored in LLM agents where dynamic content and evolving delegation complicate continuous auditing and effective revocation. <cite id="7717e9ee-2">System designs that add auditing and privilege grouping improve transparency but are not yet standard across platforms</cite>.

Bottom line
The core traditional property not currently demonstrated by existing LLM agent privilege mechanisms is the Principle of Least Privilege with strong compartmentalization and complete mediation: agents do not enforce per‑action authorization with isolation between trust domains, enabling prompt‑injection–driven privilege escalation and confused‑deputy misuse with high success rates in realistic settings. <cite id="ed9b325f-3">LLM agents lack compartmentalization and least‑privilege policies and default to a single principal with full tool access</cite> <cite id="7717e9ee-0">per‑call authorization is absent, leaving runtime authority to untrusted outputs</cite> <cite id="87050a50-0">mixed untrusted inputs in a single context bypass privilege isolation, enabling unauthorized escalation</cite> <cite id="ed9b325f-1">empirical evaluations show 84.8% attack success in privilege‑sensitive scenarios</cite>. Addressing this requires per‑call authorization, scoped capabilities with fail‑closed defaults, revocable delegation, and robust audit/containment across all tool boundaries. <cite id="7717e9ee-1">Per‑call authorization and fail‑closed controls mitigate confused deputy risks and enforce least privilege</cite> <cite id="7717e9ee-3">bounded, auditable, non‑accumulative authority with revocation</cite> <cite id="87050a50-4">privilege separation via isolation and tokens</cite>. </answer>

Title: Evaluating Privilege Usage of Agents with Real-World Tools
Snippet: In this paper, we present GrantBox, a framework for evaluating the security of LLM-based agents in privilege usage. GrantBox integrates real-world MCP servers and tools, and automatically generates benign and malicious requests to construct realistic, privilegesensitive evaluation scenarios. Preliminary results show that current LLMs remain vulnerable to privilege misuse, especially under prompt injection attacks.

Title: Evaluating Privilege Usage of Agents with Real-World Tools
Snippet: Equipping LLM agents with real-world tools can substantially improve productivity. However, granting agents autonomy over tool use also transfers the associated privileges to both the agent and the underlying LLM. Improper privilege usage may lead to serious consequences, including information leakage and infrastructure damage. While several benchmarks have been built to study agents' security, they often rely on pre-coded tools and restricted interaction patterns. Such crafted environments differ substantially from the real-world, making it hard to assess agents' security capabilities in critical privilege control and usage. Therefore, we propose GrantBox, a security evaluation sandbox for analyzing agent privilege usage. GrantBox automatically integrates real-world tools and allows LLM agents to invoke genuine privileges, enabling the evaluation of privilege usage under prompt injection attacks. Our results indicate that while LLMs exhibit basic security awareness and can block some direct attacks, they remain vulnerable to more sophisticated attacks, resulting in an average attack success rate of 84.80% in carefully crafted scenarios.

Title: Prompt Flow Integrity to Prevent Privilege Escalation in LLM Agents
Snippet: [46,48] For instance, an attacker who should not have access to the user's sensitive data can inject malicious data into the LLM agent context. The attacker's data turns into a malicious prompt in the LLM agent, instructing the agent to send emails or read sensitive files. Consequently, the attacker gains unauthorized access to the user's sensitive data and privileged operations, resulting in privilege escalation. 

However, due to their probabilistic nature, enforcing the Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) in LLM agents is inherently challenging. LLM agents are designed to process the entire agent context, including both trusted and untrusted data, to generate the most appropriate next action, including privileged operations. As a result, once an attacker injects untrusted data into the agent context, they can maliciously influence the agent's behavior and gain control over the privileged operations. 

Analyzing the internal architecture of current LLM agents, we identify two attack vectors, depending on the type of malicious prompt the attacker provides to the LLM agent. 

First, attackers can provide malicious prompts, which instruct the agent to call specific tools or do specific tasks, directly controlling the agent's privileged tool usage. This is similar to the code injection attack in traditional software systems, where an attacker injects malicious code into the program to execute the code with the program's privilege. Code injection attack is typically prevented by separating code and data (e.g., No-Execute (NX) bit [12], Data Execution Prevention (DEP) [37]), preventing arbitrary data from being executed as code. Attacks in this category are referred to as prompt injection attacks [26]. 

Second, attackers can provide malicious data that does not directly instruct the agent to call specific tools but rather provide passive information, which is then interpreted by the agent to determine the privileged tool usage. This attack is similar to data-only attacks [10,28] in traditional software systems, where an attacker injects malicious data that exploits existing vulnerabilities in the program to deviate the program's behavior. One difference in LLM agents is that the agent's behavior is not statically determined by the code but dynamically generated at runtime based on prompts.

Title: Prompt Flow Integrity to Prevent Privilege Escalation in LLM Agents
Snippet: The main security risk we identify in LLM agents is the noncompliance with Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) [46]. PoLP is a security principle that limits a principal's privilege to the minimum. It is commonly enforced by compartmentalization [31], which isolates principals into distinct protection domains (e.g., processes, sandboxes). Each protection domain is granted access only to the minimum set of resources and operations for its intended purpose. In general-purpose software systems, the minimum privilege is typically defined by the trust level of a principal. For instance, in operating systems, untrusted user processes are granted a restricted set of privileges when accessing kernel resources and operations. Similarly, in web browsers, the Rule Of 2 [24] ensures that no more than two of the following conditions are simultaneously satisfied: (i) untrusted data, (ii) unsafe implementation, and (iii) high privilege. 

As a new principal in the LLM-powered computing  paradigm [49], LLM agents lack both compartmentalization and least-privilege policies. To assist users with personalized tasks, LLM agents are often connected to privileged tools that grant access to private user data (e.g., email, cloud storage, and file system). Despite the diverse privileges these tools entail, current LLM agents by default operate as a single principal with full access over all tools and data; an agent can call any tool at any time, even when the agent is potentially controlled by the attacker. This monolithic design poses significant security risks. As tools bridge LLM agents and external systems, various data from external data flow into the agent, including untrusted data from attackers. Attackers can inject data into the agent by poisoning the external systems connected with tools (e.g., web search index, email). To prevent attackers from illegally accessing user's private data, the impact of untrusted data should be carefully controlled. 

However, a such security guarantee is difficult to achieve due to the probabilistic nature of LLMs. At each LLM inference step, the LLM agent supplies the entire context, including untrusted data, to the LLM.

Title: When Lower Privileges Suffice: Investigating Over-Privileged Tool Selection in LLM Agents

snippet.text: Equipping LLM agents with real-world tools can substantially improve productivity. However, granting agents autonomy over tool use also transfers the associated privileges to both the agent and the underlying LLM. Improper privilege usage may lead to serious consequences, including information leakage and infrastructure damage. While several benchmarks have been built to study agents' security, they often rely on pre-coded tools and restricted interaction patterns. Such crafted environments differ substantially from the real-world, making it hard to assess agents' security capabilities in critical privilege control and usage. Therefore, we propose GrantBox, a security evaluation sandbox for analyzing agent privilege usage. GrantBox automatically integrates real-world tools and allows LLM agents to invoke genuine privileges, enabling the evaluation of privilege usage under prompt injection attacks. Our results indicate that while LLMs exhibit basic security awareness and can block some direct attacks, they remain vulnerable to more sophisticated attacks, resulting in an average attack success rate of 84.80% in carefully crafted scenarios.

snippet.text:
[46,48] For instance, an attacker who should not have access to the user's sensitive data can inject malicious data into the LLM agent context. The attacker's data turns into a malicious prompt in the LLM agent, instructing the agent to send emails or read sensitive files. Consequently, the attacker gains unauthorized access to the user's sensitive data and privileged operations, resulting in privilege escalation. 

However, due to their probabilistic nature, enforcing the Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) in LLM agents is inherently challenging. LLM agents are designed to process the entire agent context, including both trusted and untrusted data, to generate the most appropriate next action, including privileged operations. As a result, once an attacker injects untrusted data into the agent context, they can maliciously influence the agent's behavior and gain control over the privileged operations. 

Analyzing the internal architecture of current LLM agents, we identify two attack vectors, depending on the type of malicious prompt the attacker provides to the LLM agent. 

First, attackers can provide malicious prompts, which instruct the agent to call specific tools or do specific tasks, directly controlling the agent's privileged tool usage. This is similar to the code injection attack in traditional software systems, where an attacker injects malicious code into the program to execute the code with the program's privilege. Code injection attack is typically prevented by separating code and data (e.g., No-Execute (NX) bit [12], Data Execution Prevention (DEP) [37]), preventing arbitrary data from being executed as code. Attacks in this category are referred to as prompt injection attacks [26]. 

Second, attackers can provide malicious data that does not directly instruct the agent to call specific tools but rather provide passive information, which is then interpreted by the agent to determine the privileged tool usage. This attack is similar to data-only attacks [10,28] in traditional software systems, where an attacker injects malicious data that exploits existing vulnerabilities in the program to deviate the program's behavior. One difference in LLM agents is that the agent's behavior is not statically determined by the code but dynamically generated at runtime based on prompts.

snippet.text:
The main security risk we identify in LLM agents is the noncompliance with Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) [46]. PoLP is a security principle that limits a principal's privilege to the minimum. It is commonly enforced by compartmentalization [31], which isolates principals into distinct protection domains (e.g., processes, sandboxes). Each protection domain is granted access only to the minimum set of resources and operations for its intended purpose. In general-purpose software systems, the minimum privilege is typically defined by the trust level of a principal. For instance, in operating systems, untrusted user processes are granted a restricted set of privileges when accessing kernel resources and operations. Similarly, in web browsers, the Rule Of 2 [24] ensures that no more than two of the following conditions are simultaneously satisfied: (i) untrusted data, (ii) unsafe implementation, and (iii) high privilege. 

As a new principal in the LLM-powered computing  paradigm [49], LLM agents lack both compartmentalization and least-privilege policies. To assist users with personalized tasks, LLM agents are often connected to privileged tools that grant access to private user data (e.g., email, cloud storage, and file system). Despite the diverse privileges these tools entail, current LLM agents by default operate as a single principal with full access over all tools and data; an agent can call any tool at any time, even when the agent is potentially controlled by the attacker. This monolithic design poses significant security risks. As tools bridge LLM agents and external systems, various data from external data flow into the agent, including untrusted data from attackers. Attackers can inject data into the agent by poisoning the external systems connected with tools (e.g., web search index, email). To prevent attackers from illegally accessing user's private data, the impact of untrusted data should be carefully controlled. 

However, a such security guarantee is difficult to achieve due to the probabilistic nature of LLMs. At each LLM inference step, the LLM agent supplies the entire context, including untrusted data, to the LLM.

Title: The Landscape of Prompt Injection Threats in LLM Agents: From Taxonomy to Analysis
Snippet: Input to the LLM agents. Within this loop, the LLM agents take inputs from various sources, along with their influence on the actions of LLM agents. Unlike computer programs, which provide isolated input interfaces for diverse inputs, LLM agents manage all the inputs in a single context memory. Different inputs are segmented with separators (e.g., "[SYS-TEM]", "[DATA]", etc.) in the context memory. We categorize the input into 3 types as shown in Fig. 1: 1 Trusted prompt input. The system prompt and user prompt constitute the basic input of an LLM agent. Among them, the system prompt is defined by the agentic developer, while the user prompt is issued by the user. The prompts are generally considered trusted in LLM agents. 

2 Untrusted tool observation. Another type of input is tool observation, originating from the tool execution process within the environment. Since the executive environment is not fully controlled by the agent, the tool observation is considered to be the untrusted input. 

3 Supply-chain dataset input. In addition to the 2 common-seen input types, the supply-chain data, including the retrieval content of RAG and the training dataset, are also considered. Most works treat these inputs as trusted; however, some threat models account for attack surfaces from the 2 data sources [63,90,91]. Thus, we label these 2 inputs as partially trusted. These inputs have different trust levels and co-exist in a single context memory of the LLM agent to affect its behaviors. 

Principles of prompt injection. The prompt injection vulnerability arises from the lack of privilege isolation between different trust levels' inputs. Despite textual delimiters, the model processes the context as a unified semantic sequence, creating ambiguity where untrusted inputs can mimic trusted input to manipulate the agent's behaviors. This results in attention competition: adversarial payloads manipulate the selfattention mechanism, shifting attention weights away from system prompts toward malicious inputs [29,93]. Furthermore, this leads to unauthorized privilege escalation, enabling the hijacking of the agent's control flow.

Title: IBAC Mathematics and Mechanics: The Case for 'Integer Based Access Control' of Data Security in the Age of AI and AI Automation
Snippet: 3 IBAC Process Dominance -Extending the trusted system's model 

We made the point earlier that moving away from the mathematically sound trusted Bell-LaPadula and Biba models to build access control systems such as ABAC and CapBAC, which lack a solid mathematical foundation, was a mistake. Instead, extending the Bell-LaPadula and Biba mathematics to enhance robustness and introduce flexibility should have been the focus. 

From now on, when we refer to Bell-LaPadula, we refer to Bell-LaPadula including the Biba model as well. 

We outline an approach here to extend Bell-LaPadula based on some mathematical research that was developed in the 1990s (see Hargraves). 

Hargraves makes the point in his master's dissertation that Bell-LaPadula can be made more flexible if both the Subject dominates the Object and the Process dominates the Object. 

This is an interesting philosophical shift. The argument being a Subject can only gain access to an Object by some Process, so why is the Process itself not part of the dominance relation and not part of the Bell-LaPadula trusted system model. 

Hargraves [12] indicates that both the Subject and the Process should dominate the object 

We will show that by adding the additional process constraint to the Bell-LaPadula model, the model becomes much more flexible and addresses the original disadvantages of Bell-LaPadula that led to the development of ABAC and CapBAC. 

We describe the extended Bell-LaPadula model and the associated proof using category theory [7]. Category theory is an abstraction of the predicate logic that enables us to express more efficiently and succinctly the necessary mathematics. 

The key point to the Bell-LaPadula extension is that we introduce one-to-one (bijective) relationship mappings between the "Subject" and a "Process" which enables greater flexibility in the model when accessing "objects". 

So in addition to user as the Subject mapped to the Object, we also have combinations of Subjects and Processes, as tuples mapped to the object. 

For example, ("user1", "printer", "secret") and ("user2", "brief ing_room", "topsecret").

This model is mainly used to mitigate the problems of confidentiality and control of access to information. In this model the subjects and the objects are classified by security rank, this avoids that the information of a high level can be of access by a subject of low level. 

By enforcing a Bell-LaPadula model policy, a subject can have access to an object, if and only if the subject is authorized to access the object by both the multi-level security policy and the control policy discretionary access.

Title: Capability Gates Are Not Authorization: Confused-Deputy Failures in LLM Agent Frameworks
Snippet: Prompt injection and agent benchmarks. Indirect prompt injection against LLM-integrated applications is established by Greshake et al. and subsequent work [5]. AgentDojo, InjecAgent, ToolEmu, and WASP provide benchmark environments for tool-using or web agents under adversarial instructions [6], [7], [8], [9]. They motivate the threat; this paper studies whether common frameworks mediate the resulting tool call by default. 

Least privilege and complete mediation. MiniScope and related least-privilege agent work are direct conceptual neighbors [10]. Classical systems security already gives the principle: every access to authority must be mediated, and confused deputies arise when authority and designation are conflated [1], [2]. SCOPEGATE operationalizes this principle at the LLM tool-call boundary. 

Agentic payment protocols. Agent-payment work, including the AP2-break line cited here, shows that payment protocols and consent artifacts do not by themselves eliminate promptinjection risk [11]. Our claim is compatible with cryptographic payment consent: even strong payment rails need a deterministic control plane that checks model-proposed transactions against operator policy before execution. 

Positioning. We do not claim "first per-call authorization for agents." MiniScope arXiv:2512.11147 exists, and the broader least-privilege principle is older than LLM agents. The defended novelty is narrower: to our knowledge, and bounded to the audited frameworks, this is the first reproducible crossframework audit of the default gap "capability gating shipped, per-call authorization absent," paired with measured model exposure and a deployable fail-closed control.

documents.title: The Landscape of Prompt Injection Threats in LLM Agents: From Taxonomy to Analysis
documents.snippet:
Input to the LLM agents. Within this loop, the LLM agents take inputs from various sources, along with their influence on the actions of LLM agents. Unlike computer programs, which provide isolated input interfaces for diverse inputs, LLM agents manage all the inputs in a single context memory. Different inputs are segmented with separators (e.g., "[SYS-TEM]", "[DATA]", etc.) in the context memory. We categorize the input into 3 types as shown in Fig. 1: 1 Trusted prompt input. The system prompt and user prompt constitute the basic input of an LLM agent. Among them, the system prompt is defined by the agentic developer, while the user prompt is issued by the user. The prompts are generally considered trusted in LLM agents. 

2 Untrusted tool observation. Another type of input is tool observation, originating from the tool execution process within the environment. Since the executive environment is not fully controlled by the agent, the tool observation is considered to be the untrusted input. 

3 Supply-chain dataset input. In addition to the 2 common-seen input types, the supply-chain data, including the retrieval content of RAG and the training dataset, are also considered. Most works treat these inputs as trusted; however, some threat models account for attack surfaces from the 2 data sources [63,90,91]. Thus, we label these 2 inputs as partially trusted. These inputs have different trust levels and co-exist in a single context memory of the LLM agent to affect its behaviors. 

Principles of prompt injection. The prompt injection vulnerability arises from the lack of privilege isolation between different trust levels' inputs. Despite textual delimiters, the model processes the context as a unified semantic sequence, creating ambiguity where untrusted inputs can mimic trusted input to manipulate the agent's behaviors. This results in attention competition: adversarial payloads manipulate the selfattention mechanism, shifting attention weights away from system prompts toward malicious inputs [29,93]. Furthermore, this leads to unauthorized privilege escalation, enabling the hijacking of the agent's control flow.

documents.title: IBAC Mathematics and Mechanics: The Case for 'Integer Based Access Control' of Data Security in the Age of AI and AI Automation
documents.snippet:
3 IBAC Process Dominance -Extending the trusted system's model 

We made the point earlier that moving away from the mathematically sound trusted Bell-LaPadula and Biba models to build access control systems such as ABAC and CapBAC, which lack a solid mathematical foundation, was a mistake. Instead, extending the Bell-LaPadula and Biba mathematics to enhance robustness and introduce flexibility should have been the focus. 

From now on, when we refer to Bell-LaPadula, we refer to Bell-LaPadula including the Biba model as well. 

We outline an approach here to extend Bell-LaPadula based on some mathematical research that was developed in the 1990s (see Hargraves). 

Hargraves makes the point in his master's dissertation that Bell-LaPadula can be made more flexible if both the Subject dominates the Object and the Process dominates the Object. 

This is an interesting philosophical shift. The argument being a Subject can only gain access to an Object by some Process, so why is the Process itself not part of the dominance relation and not part of the Bell-LaPadula trusted system model. 

Hargraves [12] indicates that both the Subject and the Process should dominate the object 

We will show that by adding the additional process constraint to the Bell-LaPadula model, the model becomes much more flexible and addresses the original disadvantages of Bell-LaPadula that led to the development of ABAC and CapBAC. 

We describe the extended Bell-LaPadula model and the associated proof using category theory [7]. Category theory is an abstraction of the predicate logic that enables us to express more efficiently and succinctly the necessary mathematics. 

The key point to the Bell-LaPadula extension is that we introduce one-to-one (bijective) relationship mappings between the "Subject" and a "Process" which enables greater flexibility in the model when accessing "objects". 

So in addition to user as the Subject mapped to the Object, we also have combinations of Subjects and Processes, as tuples mapped to the object. 

For example, ("user1", "printer", "secret") and ("user2", "brief ing_room", "topsecret").

Title: Capability Gates Are Not Authorization: Confused-Deputy Failures in LLM Agent Frameworks
Snippet: LLM agents are increasingly deployed as software components that read untrusted text and then invoke tools with real authority. A support agent may read email and refund payments; a sales agent may update CRM records; a workflow agent may call infrastructure APIs; a payment assistant may generate or modify money-moving requests. 

The core security question is not whether the model can be prompted to behave badly. Indirect prompt injection is already established. The narrower systems question is: when a compromised model emits a tool call, what does the runtime do next? 

This paper studies a specific authorization failure mode: capability gating is present, but per-call authorization is absent. Capability gating answers which tools are exposed to an agent. Per-call authorization answers whether this concrete call, with these argument values, in this principal and session context, is allowed. If a runtime exposes issue_refund and then accepts the model's well-typed amount, destination, or payment_intent as sufficient authority, it has delegated the authorization decision to an untrusted parser. 

That is the classic confused-deputy pattern: a privileged component is induced by attacker-controlled input to misuse its authority [2], [1]. Figure 1 summarizes why the distinction matters operationally: cost-optimized deployment-tier models show materially higher ASR task than flagship models in this measured sweep by mean ASR task (no paired CI for the tier aggregate), although high outliers exist in both groups. Each dot is one measured model, and the short horizontal segments mark tier means. The deployment-tier grouping is an economics/deployment inference over cost-optimized models suitable for high-volume agent traffic, not a claim about any provider's internal production fleet. ASR is the model's attempted unauthorized action under sandboxed tooling, not a breach rate. 

We make the claim deliberately narrow. We do not claim to discover prompt injection, and we do not claim the first least-privilege or per-call authorization design for agents. Prior work such as MiniScope, AgentDojo, InjecAgent, ToolEmu, and WASP already covers adjacent ground [10], [6], [7], [8], [9].

Title: AI based Operating System
Snippet: The access manager coordinates access control operations among different agents by managing a dedicated privilege group for each agent. Agents excluded from an agent's privilege group are denied access to its resources, such as interaction history. Title: Authorization Propagation in Multi-Agent AI Systems: Identity Governance as Infrastructure
Snippet: When a human principal h initiates a workflow that involves agents a 1 , a 2 , . . . , a n , the system must determine the effective authority at each agent. The naive approach -each agent inherits the initiating human's full authority -violates least privilege. The conservative approach -each agent operates only under its own service identity -may be insufficient to complete the workflow. 

The problem is to define a delegation model where: 

• Each agent's effective authority is bounded and auditable 

• Authority does not accumulate through delegation chains (no privilege escalation) 

• The initiating principal's authorization is necessary but not sufficient for downstream access 

• Delegation can be revoked at any point in the chain 

No widely deployed authorization system provides a complete solution to this in the context of autonomous agent-to-agent delegation. The confused deputy problem -where an agent is tricked into misusing its authority on behalf of an unauthorized principal -is a classical formulation of this failure mode, and has been identified in multi-agent LLM systems specifically [Anonymous, 2026f]. However, emerging work on invocation-bound capability tokens [Prakash, 2026] and postquantum delegation chains [Chen, 2026] demonstrates that the token-level mechanisms are feasible. Prakash [2026] achieves 0.049ms per-boundary verification with append-only attenuation, and Chen [2026] provides Tamarin-verified revocation within one second. What remains is integration into a workflow-scoped authorization architecture.

Title: The Attack and Defense Landscape of Agentic AI: A Comprehensive Survey
Snippet: Following the principle of least privilege, traditional security enforces privilege separation by assigning different privilege levels to different software components, exemplified by earlier automation attempts [18]. In agents, this concept extends to assigning privileges to different components and isolating these components to minimize the overall risk to the system. Design Dimensions. Privilege separation designs vary by separation policy and scope. 

A separation policy can be designed in vertical and horizontal directions. Vertical separation divides components into hierarchical privilege levels, where higher-privilege components (e.g., trusted planners) have more authority than lower-privilege components (e.g., untrusted data processors). Similar to kernel-user separation in operating systems, planner-processor separation designs [5,28,31,67,79,166,168] isolate tool call planning (high privilege) from tool result processing (low privilege). Memory minimization [11] separates the data minimizer (high privilege) from the untrusted data processing unit (low privilege). Horizontal separation partitions the system into parallel components with equal privileges but isolated access scopes. For example, per-application or per-functionality agents [78,170] each interact only with their dedicated tools and resources, preventing cross-domain exploitation. 

The scope of privilege separation indicates the component being separated. An LLM can be separated into planning tool calls and processing results [28,31,67,168], preventing tool results from directly influencing planning decisions. Memory separation [11] creates separate memory spaces, protecting sensitive data from lower-privilege components. Agents can separate external environments to enforce least-privilege [67,78,170], leveraging sandboxing, containerization [84-86], and access tokens [52,145]. 

Limitations and Open Challenges. Current privilege separation research primarily addresses generic indirect prompt injection in simplified environments [32]. It often fails to address real-world environment risks that present diverse and complex challenges requiring specialized separation strategies, such as web, file systems, and databases. Privilege separation entails utility loss by splitting functionality across isolated components. Dividing an agent into an effective set of least-privilege components remains an open challenge. Designing efficient communication across isolated components to reduce utility loss while maintaining security guarantees presents ongoing challenges for practical deployment.

Memory minimization [11] separates the data minimizer (high privilege) from the untrusted data processing unit (low privilege). Horizontal separation partitions the system into parallel components with equal privileges but isolated access scopes. For example, per-application or per-functionality agents [78,170] each interact only with their dedicated tools and resources, preventing cross-domain exploitation. 

The scope of privilege separation indicates the component being separated. An LLM can be separated into planning tool calls and processing results [28,31,67,168], preventing tool results from directly influencing planning decisions. Memory separation [11] creates separate memory spaces, protecting sensitive data from lower-privilege components. Agents can separate external environments to enforce least-privilege [67,78,170], leveraging sandboxing, containerization [84-86], and access tokens [52,145]. 

Limitations and Open Challenges. Current privilege separation research primarily addresses generic indirect prompt injection in simplified environments [32]. It often fails to address real-world environment risks that present diverse and complex challenges requiring specialized separation strategies, such as web, file systems, and databases. Privilege separation entails utility loss by splitting functionality across isolated components. Dividing an agent into an effective set of least-privilege components remains an open challenge. Designing efficient communication across isolated components to reduce utility loss while maintaining security guarantees presents ongoing challenges for practical deployment.

attempts.answer:
Overview and framing

Traditional privilege audit mechanisms assume that, given identical inputs and policy state, a system will produce the same authorization decision and outcome, enabling deterministic logging, replay, and blame assignment. These mechanisms depend on decision logs being both faithful to policy enforcement and exactly reproducible: auditors must verify that a decision would be identical on rerun to rule out policy instability or covert channels, and to attribute access to specific privileges and conditions rather than to stochastic variance. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Audit-replayability explicitly requires constraining oracles to deterministic procedures and records structured inputs, method, and sources so an auditor can re-execute and compare verdicts</cite>. <cite id="6d3b32c7-2">Regulatory guidance and risk frameworks prioritize consistency under identical inputs for auditability and examination</cite>. Against this backdrop, the stochastic nature of many LLM-based inference pipelines fundamentally undermines these determinism assumptions.

Why LLM inference is intrinsically stochastic

Modern LLMs generate text by sampling from a probability distribution over next tokens at each step, with decoding strategies such as temperature scaling, top-k, and nucleus (top-p) controlling the shape of this distribution and introducing randomness. <cite id="650c6766-0">Decoding-induced stochasticity—combined with temperature, top-k, and nucleus sampling—makes iterative generation probabilistic and compounds over sequence length</cite>. <cite id="650c6766-1">Greedy search can yield repetition and low-quality text, while top-k/top-p sampling increase diversity by drawing from truncated or reweighted distributions, and temperature governs the peakiness of the sampling distribution</cite>. <cite id="650c6766-2">The impact of decoding strategy on output quality is large; greedy/beam search yields accurate but degenerate text, while pure sampling yields varied but often incoherent text, motivating nucleus sampling to manage the unreliable tail</cite>. <cite id="650c6766-3">Sampling-based decoding relies on randomness (e.g., top-k), and beam search (optimize for high-probability output) leads to degenerate distributions; nucleus sampling dynamically contracts/expands the candidate pool to balance quality and stability</cite>.

Beyond sampling, nondeterminism arises from numerical precision, hardware execution, and provider-side changes. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Hosted LLMs do not yield bit-identical outputs even at temperature 0 with a fixed seed due to floating-point nondeterminism in batched GPU inference, sparse MoE routing variability, and silent backend updates that are not version-pinned by the provider</cite>. <cite id="650c6766-4">Sources of nondeterminism include random seeds, sampling procedures, numerical precision, and hardware execution; average performance metrics can mask configuration-dependent instability and individual-input variability</cite>. <cite id="1fd158d1-0">Identical prompts can yield varying responses due to probabilistic outputs conditioned on sampling parameters like temperature, complicating traceability, testing, and verification</cite>. Empirically, this variability persists even when variance controls are maxed out. <cite id="1fd158d1-4">Across multiple LLMs, identical prompts with minimal output variability settings still produced inconsistent outputs; while some settings show high short-term reliability, proprietary models that change over time lack guarantees of long-term reliability, motivating explicit use of seed parameters to fix randomness in local/open models (and emerging support in proprietary APIs)</cite>. <cite id="1fd158d1-2">Temperature zero does not guarantee byte-level determinism with live APIs; floating-point rounding in the sampler and batch-effect variation introduce bounded residual drift on the order of a few tokens, compressing under pinned model versions but not fully eliminating nondeterminism</cite>.

How nondeterminism violates audit determinism assumptions

Privilege audits assume deterministic decision functions so that:
- Given a request, role/permission set, and policy version, the decision is uniquely determined and can be logged exactly for later verification.
- Replay on the same inputs yields the same decision, enabling forensic reconstruction and “what would happen if re-run?” demonstrations to regulators.

LLM-based oracles and gatekeepers break these assumptions in three key ways.

First, same-inputs, different outputs make decision logs unreliable as evidence of policy behavior. <cite id="1fd158d1-0">Because outputs are probabilistic under temperature and sampling, identical prompts yield varying responses, undermining traceability, testing, and verification</cite>. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Modern hosted LLMs do not produce bit-identical outputs even with temperature 0 and a fixed seed due to floating-point and backend factors, so raw logs cannot guarantee determinism; audit-replayability therefore requires recording structured inputs and allowing re-execution to compare original and re-executed verdicts</cite>. Without bit-identical replay, an auditor cannot rule out that a “policy violation” was actually sampling variance, and cannot attribute decisions uniquely to privileges and rules rather than noise.

Second, uncontrolled hardware/implementation and provider updates introduce stateful “silent” non-determinism. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Batched GPU floating-point non-determinism and MoE routing variability change the effective evaluation path even when the model identifier and inputs are fixed</cite>, while <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">silent backend updates not version-pinned by the provider further alter the decision function over time</cite>. Such changes violate the audit assumption that policy artifacts (decision logs) correspond to a fixed, audited decision procedure. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Strict offline re-verifiability requires constraining oracles to deterministic procedures and versioning the inference runtime</cite>.

Third, auditability is not the same as raw logging; policy binding must capture evaluation context and method. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Audit-replayability differs from raw logging: structured inputs, inference method, and sources are recorded so an auditor can recover which rule applied and whether re-execution yields the same verdict</cite>. With LLMs, even if one logs prompts and tokens verbatim, the downstream decision may differ on rerun due to numerical and implementation drift, and the model may change its mind without violating its own policy content. <cite id="6d3b32c7-3">Authorization logs that bind decisions to exact evaluation contexts enable forensic reconstruction and policy evolution without reliance on agent internals; traditional effect logs alone cannot answer why a decision was allowed</cite>. This gap means traditional privilege audits that rely on effect-only logs cannot verify that the same policy inputs would yield the same decision.

Implications for privilege auditing and security analysis

The stochastic nature of LLM inference directly undermines standard privilege audit workflows:
- Determinism checks and stability tests fail. <cite id="1fd158d1-0">Non-deterministic outputs prevent preserving reproducible input–output pairs for audit and replay</cite>; <cite id="6d3b32c7-2">a model with 50% determinism cannot satisfy regulatory examinations that require identical classifications under identical inputs</cite>.
- Causality and blame assignment become brittle. <cite id="6d3b32c7-3">Traditional audit logs record effects (API calls, state mutations) but not why they were allowed; to determine privilege effects, systems must log binding decisions with evaluation context</cite>. With LLM oracles, the “why” is intertwined with stochastic sampling, making it hard to apportion blame to privilege entitlements versus model noise.
- Temporal validity and versioning are critical. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Silent provider updates and runtime variability mean the same decision artifact can map to different procedures over time; auditors need pinned model/runtime identifiers and method records to ensure offline re-verifiability</cite>.
- Risk and compliance cannot assume explainability by local inference. <cite id="6d3b32c7-2">Supervisory guidance, EU AI Act auditability requirements, and NIST RMF emphasize consistent decisions under identical inputs to support explainability and reproducibility</cite>, which LLM-based decision-making cannot guarantee by default.

Mitigations and design patterns for auditable LLM use

Despite intrinsic randomness, several patterns restore auditability by constraining variability at the decision boundary:
- Deterministic oracles and replayable procedures. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Deployments can adopt deterministic oracles that implement auditable decision rules, preserving the wire format and audit-trail while removing stochastic drift</cite>. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Audit-replayability captures structured inputs and inference method so auditors can compare original and re-executed verdicts even if full bit-identicalness is impractical</cite>.
- Deterministic projection with quantified residual noise. <cite id="1fd158d1-2">Stateless decision projection treats decisions as a pure function of inputs and model version, with temperature zero producing equality up to API-level residual nondeterminism; residual drift from floating-point and batch effects is bounded and compresses under pinned versions, enabling deterministic replay of the decision surface while acknowledging limited token-level variability</cite>.
- Schema-first and deterministic validation for policy pipelines. <cite id="6d3b32c7-4">Schema induction/fusion pipelines quantify LLM nondeterminism via repeated runs and deterministically validate and score outputs using controllable checks (JSON validity, coverage, structural consistency), logging reward breakdowns and validation failures for auditing and reproducibility</cite>.
- Version pinning, seeds, and controlled decoding. <cite id="1fd158d1-4">Use seed parameters and low temperature to stabilize outputs where feasible, and pin model weights and inference runtimes to reduce residual nondeterminism</cite>. <cite id="1fd158d1-3">Lower temperature increases consistency, and systematic sweeps with multiple samples can identify stable outputs; making prompts and outputs public improves reproducibility</cite>.
- Log what must be logged: structured decisions, not raw tokens. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Record structured premises, conclusions, inference_method, and source bindings rather than the prompt blob, enabling replay and rule attribution independent of bit-identical outputs</cite>. <cite id="6d3b32c7-3">Authorization logs bind decisions to evaluation context and policy version to support append-only, causally ordered forensic reconstruction</cite>.

Putting it together: Why nondeterminism violates the reproducibility assumption

Traditional privilege audits assume a deterministic decision function so that identical requests, roles, and timestamps map to a unique decision and log entry, enabling replay and blame assignment. <cite id="6d3b32c7-2">Regulatory and risk frameworks codify this by prioritizing consistency under identical inputs as the bar for auditability and model risk control</cite>, and practical systems operationalize this through replayable decision logs and versioned artifacts. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">LLMs break this assumption because their inference kernels are stochastic: sampling distributions over tokens (temperature, top-k/top-p), numerical and hardware effects, and provider-side changes cause the same inputs to yield different outputs even with seeds and low temperatures</cite>. Consequently, identical prompts and privilege contexts do not guarantee identical outcomes, so effect-only logs cannot answer why a decision was allowed, and “would-be-the-same-on-replay” demonstrations cannot be guaranteed. <cite id="1fd158d1-0">Non-deterministic outputs make traceability, testing, and verification harder, requiring provenance capture of inputs, metadata, and context if audits are to be reliable</cite>. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Modern hosted LLMs thus require audit-replayability designs that log structured inputs and allow re-execution to compare verdicts, or adopt deterministic oracles with pinned runtimes to restore determinism at the decision boundary</cite>.

In short, the stochastic mechanics of LLM inference—probabilistic token selection compounded over sequence length, sensitivity to numerical precision and hardware, and mutable backend implementations—undermine the foundational determinism of traditional privilege audits. Audits that depend on bit-identical replay and unique input–output mappings cannot assume these properties for LLM-based oracles without explicit determinism constraints, version pinning, and structured decision logging. <cite id="650c6766-0">Decoding-induced stochasticity and system-level nondeterminism are central to deployments</cite>, and <cite id="650c6766-4">stochastic training/inference has long been recognized as a reproducibility challenge</cite>, making this a structural mismatch that must be addressed with protocol-level and architectural mitigations to make privilege auditing meaningful again. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Audit-replayability is not raw logging; it requires deterministic procedures and versioned inference</cite>, and <cite id="1fd158d1-2">bounded residual nondeterminism can be managed but not eliminated by default</cite>.

Title: Local Normalization Distortion and the Thermodynamic Formalism of Decoding Strategies for Large Language Models
Snippet: Autoregressive large-language models are poised to transform industries such as healthcare, finance and education (Zhao et al., 2024). Rapid advancements in this field have been fueled by scaling (Hoffmann et al., 2024), transformer network architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017), and alignment processes (Christiano et al., 2017;Rafailov et al., 2024). However, autoregressive language models produce conditional distributions over predicted next tokens, and these must be iteratively sampled during inference. A suite of decoding methods exist * Equal contribution. 

for this sampling, such as top-k, nucleus, or temperature sampling, but these are based on heuristics and our understanding of these methods is in its infancy, with most being developed through trial and error (Wiher et al., 2022). This is surprising, since the choice of decoding strategy has a profound impact on the quality of the generated text and, in some cases, may be more important than the model architecture (Wiher et al., 2022). For example, greedy sampling, or the related concept of beam search, tends to produce accurate but repetitive or dull text (Holtzman et al., 2020). In contrast, pure sampling produces much more varied and interesting text but can produce text which is 'incoherent and almost unrelated to the context' (Holtzman et al., 2020). 

Our primary goal is to fill this gap and initiate the theoretical study of decoding strategies. As an application of this theory, we investigate a wellknown defect of popular decoding strategies, which results from truncating the distribution of possible next tokens at each step during inference. Truncation necessitates repeated renormalization to obtain valid probability distributions, and results in a phenomenon we term local normalization distortion. The fact that local normalization distorts the resulting probability distribution is well-known, but not well-understood.

Indeed, language models do generally assign high scores to well-formed text, yet the highest scores for longer texts are often generic, repetitive, and awkward. Figure 2 exposes how different the distribution of probabilities assigned to beam search decoded text and naturally occurring text really are. 

Perhaps equally surprising is the right side of Figure 1, which shows that pure sampling -sampling directly from the probabilities predicted by the model -results in text that is incoherent and almost unrelated to the context. Why is text produced by pure sampling so degenerate? In this work we show that the "unreliable tail" is to blame. This unreliable tail is composed of tens of thousands of candidate tokens with relatively low probability that are over-represented in the aggregate. 

To overcome these issues we introduce Nucleus Sampling ( §3.1). The key intuition of Nucleus Sampling is that the vast majority of probability mass at each time step is concentrated in the nucleus, a small subset of the vocabulary that tends to range between one and a thousand candidates. Instead of relying on a fixed top-k, or using a temperature parameter to control the shape of the distribution without sufficiently suppressing the unreliable tail, we propose sampling from the top-p portion of the probability mass, expanding and contracting the candidate pool dynamically.

This ordering model reflects a deliberate trade-off: per-domain determinism and causal consistency are sufficient for auditability and replay, while global ordering would conflate unrelated decision streams and obscure causality behind wall-clock artifacts. 

Why This Is Not an Event Log. Traditional audit and observability systems record effects: API calls, state mutations, and network requests. Such logs answer the question what happened. They do not, and cannot, answer why it was allowed. [7], [16]. 

The Faramesh audit log records authorization decisions, not side effects. Each record captures the binding: 

freezing the exact evaluation context at decision time. This binding is the authorization boundary itself. Execution logs may later confirm that an effect occurred, but only decision records can establish whether that effect was authorized, under which policy, and with what assumptions. 

Observability systems operate downstream of execution. Provenance systems operate at the boundary between intent and effect. Faramesh records the latter [12], [18]. 

This distinction is architectural, not operational. 

Summary. The audit log architecture defined here elevates authorization decisions to first-class, replayable system artifacts. By logging canonical actions, evaluation context, and outcomes in an append-only, causally ordered structure, Faramesh enables forensic reconstruction and policy evolution without reliance on agent internals or execution systems. Title: A Primer for Evaluating Large Language Models in Social-Science Research
Snippet: LLMs pose unique challenges because of their nondeterministic nature. An LLM may code a piece of text differently each time it is asked to even when using the same prompts and model settings. For example, Astekin et al. (2024) provided a detailed case study on inconsistencies in an LLM's outputs when responding to identical prompts with the same model settings. They observed this tendency across various LLMs (e.g., GPT, LLaMA, Claude). In their study, the authors repeatedly provided an LLM with status messages (called "logs") and asked the model to process it in line with a template. Across all models, they found inconsistent outputs even when the model parameters are set to minimal output variability. 

Of course, not all LLM applications are unreliable. Rathje et al. (2024) reported a Cohen's kappa of more than .90 when querying ChatGPT 1 day apart and across prompts translated into different languages, showing that in some cases, LLMs can be highly reliable and robust. However, especially with proprietary models that change over time, there is no guarantee of long-term reliability. Researchers should thus ensure that their findings are reliable and not coincidental at the time of their studies. 

To improve reproducibility, researchers can use "seed" parameters. These parameters govern the random elements in the LLM's output-generation process, ensuring consistent results across different runs. It is analogous to providing the LLM with a specific starting point on a map. By setting a seed parameter, researchers essentially fix this starting point so that the LLM will follow the same route and arrive at the same destination (i.e., produce the same output) every time it encounters the same prompt with the same seed. This functionality is typically available in locally run open-source models. Recently, even some proprietary models have begun to incorporate it, as seen in OpenAI's current testing of seed parameters (for OpenAI's beta testing of the seed parameter, see OpenAI, 2023).

Overview and framing

Traditional privilege audit mechanisms assume that, given identical inputs and policy state, a system will produce the same authorization decision and outcome, enabling deterministic logging, replay, and blame assignment. These mechanisms depend on decision logs being both faithful to policy enforcement and exactly reproducible: auditors must verify that a decision would be identical on rerun to rule out policy instability or covert channels, and to attribute access to specific privileges and conditions rather than to stochastic variance. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Audit-replayability explicitly requires constraining oracles to deterministic procedures and records structured inputs, method, and sources so an auditor can re-execute and compare verdicts</cite>. <cite id="6d3b32c7-2">Regulatory guidance and risk frameworks prioritize consistency under identical inputs for auditability and examination</cite>. Against this backdrop, the stochastic nature of many LLM-based inference pipelines fundamentally undermines these determinism assumptions.

Why LLM inference is intrinsically stochastic

Modern LLMs generate text by sampling from a probability distribution over next tokens at each step, with decoding strategies such as temperature scaling, top-k, and nucleus (top-p) controlling the shape of this distribution and introducing randomness. <cite id="650c6766-0">Decoding-induced stochasticity—combined with temperature, top-k, and nucleus sampling—makes iterative generation probabilistic and compounds over sequence length</cite>. <cite id="650c6766-1">Greedy search can yield repetition and low-quality text, while top-k/top-p sampling increase diversity by drawing from truncated or reweighted distributions, and temperature governs the peakiness of the sampling distribution</cite>. <cite id="650c6766-2">The impact of decoding strategy on output quality is large; greedy/beam search yields accurate but degenerate text, while pure sampling yields varied but often incoherent text, motivating nucleus sampling to manage the unreliable tail</cite>. <cite id="650c6766-3">Sampling-based decoding relies on randomness (e.g., top-k), and beam search (optimize for high-probability output) leads to degenerate distributions; nucleus sampling dynamically contracts/expands the candidate pool to balance quality and stability</cite>.

Beyond sampling, nondeterminism arises from numerical precision, hardware execution, and provider-side changes. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Hosted LLMs do not yield bit-identical outputs even at temperature 0 with a fixed seed due to floating-point nondeterminism in batched GPU inference, sparse MoE routing variability, and silent backend updates that are not version-pinned by the provider</cite>. <cite id="650c6766-4">Sources of nondeterminism include random seeds, sampling procedures, numerical precision, and hardware execution; average performance metrics can mask configuration-dependent instability and individual-input variability</cite>. <cite id="1fd158d1-0">Identical prompts can yield varying responses due to probabilistic outputs conditioned on sampling parameters like temperature, complicating traceability, testing, and verification</cite>. Empirically, this variability persists even when variance controls are maxed out. <cite id="1fd158d1-4">Across multiple LLMs, identical prompts with minimal output variability settings still produced inconsistent outputs; while some settings show high short-term reliability, proprietary models that change over time lack guarantees of long-term reliability, motivating explicit use of seed parameters to fix randomness in local/open models (and emerging support in proprietary APIs)</cite>. <cite id="1fd158d1-2">Temperature zero does not guarantee byte-level determinism with live APIs; floating-point rounding in the sampler and batch-effect variation introduce bounded residual drift on the order of a few tokens, compressing under pinned model versions but not fully eliminating nondeterminism</cite>.

How nondeterminism violates audit determinism assumptions

Privilege audits assume deterministic decision functions so that:
- Given a request, role/permission set, and policy version, the decision is uniquely determined and can be logged exactly for later verification.
- Replay on the same inputs yields the same decision, enabling forensic reconstruction and “what would happen if re-run?” demonstrations to regulators.

LLM-based oracles and gatekeepers break these assumptions in three key ways.

First, same-inputs, different outputs make decision logs unreliable as evidence of policy behavior. <cite id="1fd158d1-0">Because outputs are probabilistic under temperature and sampling, identical prompts yield varying responses, undermining traceability, testing, and verification</cite>. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Modern hosted LLMs do not produce bit-identical outputs even with temperature 0 and a fixed seed due to floating-point and backend factors, so raw logs cannot guarantee determinism; audit-replayability therefore requires recording structured inputs and allowing re-execution to compare original and re-executed verdicts</cite>. Without bit-identical replay, an auditor cannot rule out that a “policy violation” was actually sampling variance, and cannot attribute decisions uniquely to privileges and rules rather than noise.

Second, uncontrolled hardware/implementation and provider updates introduce stateful “silent” non-determinism. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Batched GPU floating-point non-determinism and MoE routing variability change the effective evaluation path even when the model identifier and inputs are fixed</cite>, while <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">silent backend updates not version-pinned by the provider further alter the decision function over time</cite>. Such changes violate the audit assumption that policy artifacts (decision logs) correspond to a fixed, audited decision procedure. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Strict offline re-verifiability requires constraining oracles to deterministic procedures and versioning the inference runtime</cite>.

Third, auditability is not the same as raw logging; policy binding must capture evaluation context and method. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Audit-replayability differs from raw logging: structured inputs, inference method, and sources are recorded so an auditor can recover which rule applied and whether re-execution yields the same verdict</cite>. With LLMs, even if one logs prompts and tokens verbatim, the downstream decision may differ on rerun due to numerical and implementation drift, and the model may change its mind without violating its own policy content. <cite id="6d3b32c7-3">Authorization logs that bind decisions to exact evaluation contexts enable forensic reconstruction and policy evolution without reliance on agent internals; traditional effect logs alone cannot answer why a decision was allowed</cite>. This gap means traditional privilege audits that rely on effect-only logs cannot verify that the same policy inputs would yield the same decision.

Implications for privilege auditing and security analysis

The stochastic nature of LLM inference directly undermines standard privilege audit workflows:
- Determinism checks and stability tests fail. <cite id="1fd158d1-0">Non-deterministic outputs prevent preserving reproducible input–output pairs for audit and replay</cite>; <cite id="6d3b32c7-2">a model with 50% determinism cannot satisfy regulatory examinations that require identical classifications under identical inputs</cite>.
- Causality and blame assignment become brittle. <cite id="6d3b32c7-3">Traditional audit logs record effects (API calls, state mutations) but not why they were allowed; to determine privilege effects, systems must log binding decisions with evaluation context</cite>. With LLM oracles, the “why” is intertwined with stochastic sampling, making it hard to apportion blame to privilege entitlements versus model noise.
- Temporal validity and versioning are critical. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Silent provider updates and runtime variability mean the same decision artifact can map to different procedures over time; auditors need pinned model/runtime identifiers and method records to ensure offline re-verifiability</cite>.
- Risk and compliance cannot assume explainability by local inference. <cite id="6d3b32c7-2">Supervisory guidance, EU AI Act auditability requirements, and NIST RMF emphasize consistent decisions under identical inputs to support explainability and reproducibility</cite>, which LLM-based decision-making cannot guarantee by default.

Mitigations and design patterns for auditable LLM use

Despite intrinsic randomness, several patterns restore auditability by constraining variability at the decision boundary:
- Deterministic oracles and replayable procedures. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Deployments can adopt deterministic oracles that implement auditable decision rules, preserving the wire format and audit-trail while removing stochastic drift</cite>. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Audit-replayability captures structured inputs and inference method so auditors can compare original and re-executed verdicts even if full bit-identicalness is impractical</cite>.
- Deterministic projection with quantified residual noise. <cite id="1fd158d1-2">Stateless decision projection treats decisions as a pure function of inputs and model version, with temperature zero producing equality up to API-level residual nondeterminism; residual drift from floating-point and batch effects is bounded and compresses under pinned versions, enabling deterministic replay of the decision surface while acknowledging limited token-level variability</cite>.
- Schema-first and deterministic validation for policy pipelines. <cite id="6d3b32c7-4">Schema induction/fusion pipelines quantify LLM nondeterminism via repeated runs and deterministically validate and score outputs using controllable checks (JSON validity, coverage, structural consistency), logging reward breakdowns and validation failures for auditing and reproducibility</cite>.
- Version pinning, seeds, and controlled decoding. <cite id="1fd158d1-4">Use seed parameters and low temperature to stabilize outputs where feasible, and pin model weights and inference runtimes to reduce residual nondeterminism</cite>. <cite id="1fd158d1-3">Lower temperature increases consistency, and systematic sweeps with multiple samples can identify stable outputs; making prompts and outputs public improves reproducibility</cite>.
- Log what must be logged: structured decisions, not raw tokens. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Record structured premises, conclusions, inference_method, and source bindings rather than the prompt blob, enabling replay and rule attribution independent of bit-identical outputs</cite>. <cite id="6d3b32c7-3">Authorization logs bind decisions to evaluation context and policy version to support append-only, causally ordered forensic reconstruction</cite>.

Putting it together: Why nondeterminism violates the reproducibility assumption

Traditional privilege audits assume a deterministic decision function so that identical requests, roles, and timestamps map to a unique decision and log entry, enabling replay and blame assignment. <cite id="6d3b32c7-2">Regulatory and risk frameworks codify this by prioritizing consistency under identical inputs as the bar for auditability and model risk control</cite>, and practical systems operationalize this through replayable decision logs and versioned artifacts. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">LLMs break this assumption because their inference kernels are stochastic: sampling distributions over tokens (temperature, top-k/top-p), numerical and hardware effects, and provider-side changes cause the same inputs to yield different outputs even with seeds and low temperatures</cite>. Consequently, identical prompts and privilege contexts do not guarantee identical outcomes, so effect-only logs cannot answer why a decision was allowed, and “would-be-the-same-on-replay” demonstrations cannot be guaranteed. <cite id="1fd158d1-0">Non-deterministic outputs make traceability, testing, and verification harder, requiring provenance capture of inputs, metadata, and context if audits are to be reliable</cite>. <cite id="6d3b32c7-0">Modern hosted LLMs thus require audit-replayability designs that log structured inputs and allow re-execution to compare verdicts, or adopt deterministic oracles with pinned runtimes to restore determinism at the decision boundary</cite>.

In short, the stochastic mechanics of LLM inference—probabilistic token selection compounded over sequence length, sensitivity to numerical precision and hardware, and mutable backend implementations—undermine the foundational determinism of traditional privilege audits.
